metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health
metadata.summary: The excerpt addresses outcomes and limitations of treatments for short-penis complaints, then covers the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of priapism. It distinguishes ischaemic, non-ischaemic and stuttering priapism, including presentations associated with sickle cell disease and those occurring in children. Management spans urgent medical treatment, procedures, surgery and prevention of recurrent episodes.

toxicities.incidence: Ischaemic priapism occurred in 0.4-35% after intracavernosal injection of erectogenic agents. The evidence summary describes about 5% after papaverine-based combinations and < 1% after prostaglandin E1 monotherapy. PDE5Is accounted for 2.9% of reported drug-induced priapism cases in FDA Adverse Reporting System Public Dashboard data; most affected men also had other risk factors, so causation by PDE5Is remains unclear.
recognition: Persistent rigid erection, usually accompanied by progressive penile pain.

toxicities.event: Cardiovascular and neurological adverse effects of intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment
recognition: Headache, dizziness, hypertension, reflex bradycardia, tachycardia and palpitations are potential effects.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage has been reported sporadically.
A hypertensive crisis may occur when sympathomimetic agents are given with monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
prevention: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous sympathomimetic administration.
After phenylephrine injection, monitor blood pressure and pulse every fifteen minutes for 1 hour, particularly in older men with pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
Use phenylephrine cautiously in men with cardiovascular disease; the management figure advises pulse and blood-pressure monitoring during administration and for one hour afterwards.

The Guidelines Panel considers intracavernous sympathomimetic agents contraindicated in malignant or poorly controlled hypertension. The management figure also identifies a history of cerebro-vascular disease and significant hypertension as contraindications to phenylephrine.
Do not give sympathomimetic agents together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Use lower phenylephrine doses in children and patients with severe cardiovascular diseases.

toxicities.event: Local adverse effects of Methylene blue
recognition: Transient burning and blue penile discolouration.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of oral α-adrenergic agonists
recognition: Tachycardia and palpitations.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of hormonal treatment for recurrent priapism
recognition: Hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, reduced libido and asthenia are potential effects.
Hormonal agents can impair fertility through contraceptive effects and interference with sexual maturation and spermatogenesis.
The potential cardiovascular toxicity of oestrogens limits their clinical use.
prevention: Do not use hormonal therapies to prevent recurrent episodes before sexual maturation.
Seek advice from a paediatric endocrinologist when considering hormonal treatment for pre-pubertal boys or adolescents.
Counsel men attempting conception with a partner comprehensively before hormonal treatment; sperm cryopreservation may be considered to mitigate potential fertility effects of anti-androgen therapy.

recognition: Reduced libido, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion, blurred vision, headache, gynaecomastia, rash and arrhythmia.
A small double-blind, placebo-controlled study found reduced sexual desire, excitement and penile rigidity with digoxin.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects and precautions for Terbutaline
recognition: Nervousness, shakiness, drowsiness, palpitations, headache, dizziness, hot flushes, nausea and weakness.
prevention: Use cautiously in patients with coronary artery disease, increased intravascular fluid volume, oedema or hypokalaemia.

recognition: Anorgasmia and impaired erectile function.
Drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, headache, hypotension and nausea.
Oligozoospermia and leg ulcers.
Mild bleeding is the adverse effect reported most commonly.

toxicities.event: Neurological events associated with exchange transfusion
toxicities.incidence: A systematic review reported 9 cases of ASPEN syndrome following blood transfusion.
recognition: ASPEN syndrome comprises SCD, priapism, exchange transfusion and neurological events; serious neurological sequelae have also been reported.
prevention: Do not routinely use exchange transfusion as primary treatment for SCD-related priapism unless there is a risk of SCD-related symptoms.
Do not delay initial penile treatment while providing supportive measures for SCD-related priapism.

toxicities.event: Erectile dysfunction and penile damage after prolonged ischaemic priapism
toxicities.incidence: Studies cited by the guideline report ED > 90% after priapism lasting more than 36-48 hours.
recognition: Smooth muscle necrosis, corporal fibrosis, penile scarring, shortening, deformity and ED may follow prolonged ischaemia, including after apparently successful detumescence.
prevention: Begin stepwise treatment as early as possible, within four to six hours, to limit irreversible injury.
Intervention beyond 48-72 hours may relieve pain and erection but has little clinical benefit for preventing long-term ED.

recognition: Erectile-function recovery after shunting for prolonged priapism is low; outcomes relate to priapism duration, pre-operative erectile status and age.
Burnett’s technique (Snake manoeuvre) has reported wound infection, penile skin necrosis and urethrocutaneous fistulae.
Quackles’s technique may cause an unintended urethro-cavernous fistula, urethral stricture or cavernositis.
Grayhack’s procedure may cause saphenofemoral thrombus formation or pulmonary embolism.
prevention: Use distal shunts as the initial surgical approach because they are less invasive and have lower post-operative ED rates than proximal shunts.
A perineal approach to the bulb of the corpus spongiosum carries less risk of urethral injury during proximal shunting.

toxicities.event: Complications of penile prosthesis implantation after priapism
toxicities.incidence: The guideline reports infection rates of 6-7% with early implantation vs. 19-30% with late implantation, penile shortening of 3% vs. 40%, and revision rates of 9% vs. 27%, respectively.
recognition: Distal erosion, prosthetic infection, penile shortening and a need for revision surgery may occur.
An inflatable prosthesis can develop a contracting fibrous capsule if cycling does not begin immediately.
prevention: If a shunt has been performed, delay prosthesis implantation to reduce implant infection and erosion risk while oedema resolves and the wound heals.
Begin cycling an immediately inserted inflatable prosthesis immediately to prevent capsule contraction, penile curvature and shortening.
A vacuum device may be used during a post-shunt waiting period to limit fibrosis and penile shortening.

toxicities.event: Sexual dysfunction during androgen deprivation for non-ischaemic priapism
recognition: Sexual dysfunction is a consideration when these treatments are used.
prevention: Consider androgen deprivation therapy for non-ischaemic priapism only in adults.

toxicities.event: Erectile dysfunction and distal penile flaccidity during conservative management of non-ischaemic priapism
toxicities.incidence: In a cited case series of six patients with high-flow priapism, all reported ED or distal penile flaccidity after a median follow-up of 4.5 (2-12) weeks.
recognition: ED or loss of distal penile rigidity can develop while the fistula remains under conservative management.
prevention: Use close follow-up with colour duplex US and MRI to detect distal penile fibrosis and inform decisions about earlier embolisation.

toxicities.incidence: Reported ED rates after the first arterial embolization range from 0-33.3%.
recognition: Potential complications include ED, penile gangrene, gluteal ischaemia, cavernositis and perineal abscess.
prevention: The guideline recommends temporary material for the first selective arterial embolisation, while noting that evidence is insufficient to establish a sexual-function advantage over permanent material.

toxicities.event: Erectile dysfunction after surgical ligation of a fistula
associated_therapies: selective surgical ligation of the fistula
toxicities.incidence: Reported ED rates following treatment for non-ischaemic priapism range from 0-50%; surgical ligation has the highest reported rates.
recognition: ED may follow the technically challenging operation.
prevention: Reserve fistula ligation as a final option after repeated arterial embolisation has failed.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Peri-procedural anti-thrombotic treatment may reduce priapism recurrence after shunting. The evidence summary describes 325 mg acetylsalicylic acid pre-operatively, 5,000 IU heparin intra-operatively, followed by 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid and 75 mg clopidogrel post-operatively; a cited comparison found an 84% decrease in recurrence in the treated shunt group after failed aspiration.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing penile shunt surgery after failed aspiration.
prophylaxis.duration: five days postoperatively for 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid and 75 mg clopidogrel

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use hormonal therapies, mainly gonadotropin-receptor hormone agonists or antagonists, and/or anti-androgens to prevent further episodes in patients with frequent stuttering-priapism relapses; do not use them before sexual maturation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Sexually mature patients with frequent relapses of stuttering priapism.

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline describes low-dose PDE5Is as an option that can alleviate and prevent stuttering priapism, mainly in idiopathic and SCD-associated cases. Start treatment only while the penis is flaccid, not during an acute episode; an effect is delayed by one week.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with stuttering priapism, mainly those with idiopathic or SCD-associated priapism.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin or terbutaline only for frequent, uncontrolled stuttering-priapism relapses; the evidence for these systemic drugs is limited.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with frequent and uncontrolled stuttering-priapism relapses.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Oral Pseudoephedrine can be a first-line option for stuttering priapism. Studies suggest some preventive benefit from daily oral α-adrenergic agonists.
Oral Etilephrine has been used to prevent SCD-related stuttering priapism at 5-10 mg daily, with reported response rates of up to 72%.
Hydroxyurea has limited evidence suggesting a preventive role in recurrent priapism.

conditions.name: short-penis syndrome
conditions.description: A complaint of a short penis may reflect an anatomical or pathological condition, although some patients have neither. Assessment and treatment require medical and ethical consideration within a multidisciplinary approach; most reported treatment outcomes have limited supporting evidence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The complaint varies in its presentation and causes. Psychopathological symptoms may also be present and require referral for further medical diagnosis.

conditions.name: Priapism
conditions.description: An erection that persists or is prolonged without sexual stimulation and does not resolve.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain, rigidity, preceding trauma and the pattern of episodes help distinguish its forms.

subtypes.name: Ischaemic priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually involves a rigid, painful erection with little or no cavernosal arterial inflow.

subtypes.name: Non-ischaemic priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Often follows trauma and typically involves a painless erection that is not fully rigid.

subtypes.name: Stuttering priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Causes repeated, painful prolonged erections separated by periods of detumescence.

subtypes.name: neonatal priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Described as an additional form in children.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Listed among factors associated with the development of priapism.

conditions.name: Ischaemic priapism
conditions.description: A persistent erection with rigid corpora cavernosa and minimal or absent cavernosal arterial inflow. Progressive hypoxia, hypercapnia, glucopenia and acidosis develop within the corpora. Beyond 4 hours, the condition resembles a compartment syndrome and requires emergency intervention.
conditions.epidemiology: It accounts for > 95% of priapism episodes. No specific cause is identified in most cases. It may follow intracavernosal injection of erectogenic agents in 0.4-35% of cases; the reported risk after prostaglandin E1 injection is < 1%. SCD accounts for 63% of childhood cases and is the primary cause in 23% of adult cases.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The corpora are generally fully rigid and tender, the glans remains soft, and penile pain is usually severe and progressive. Erection duration is the most significant predictor of irreversible consequences, including erectile dysfunction. After 48-72 hours from onset, intervention may relieve pain and the erection but offers little clinical benefit in preventing long-term erectile dysfunction.

subtypes.name: malignant priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A rare infiltrative form associated with regional tumour invasion, metastasis or haematological malignancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the priapism subtype and possible cause.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess SCD and other haematological abnormalities; pelvic, genital or perineal trauma; erection duration and pain; prescribed and recreational drugs; previous episodes and their treatment; and erectile function before the current episode.

diagnostic_workup.test: Examination of the genitalia, perineum and abdomen
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess rigidity, tenderness and possible underlying disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Fully rigid, tender corpora with a soft glans support ischaemic priapism. Pelvic examination may reveal pelvic or genitourinary malignancy.

diagnostic_workup.test: Full blood count, white blood cell count with blood cell differential, platelet count and coagulation profile
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anaemia and detect haematological abnormalities.

diagnostic_workup.test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The first corporal aspirate is usually dark; typical ischaemic values are pO2 < 30 mmHg, pCO2 > 60 mmHg and pH < 7.25.

diagnostic_workup.test: Haemoglobinopathy screen, including haemoglobin electrophoresis when indicated
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate SCD or another haemoglobinopathy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For patients with low-flow priapism at high risk of sickle cell disease or thalassemia; further testing is guided by the history, examination and laboratory findings.

diagnostic_workup.test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism and assess cavernosal flow.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After clinical diagnosis and before corporal aspiration.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sluggish or absent cavernosal blood flow supports ischaemic priapism. Flow assessed after intervention can be misleading because of reperfusion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess cavernosal smooth-muscle viability and penile fibrosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases of prolonged or refractory ischaemic priapism, including delayed presentation (> 48 hours).
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A prospective study of 38 patients reported 100% sensitivity for predicting non-viable smooth muscle when MRI findings were compared with corpus cavernosum biopsies.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess smooth-muscle necrosis to inform decisions about immediate penile prosthesis insertion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected refractory or delayed cases (> 48 hours).
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence of necrosis suggests that shunting is likely to fail.

recommended_tests: Assessment for penile fibrosis and deformity
follow_up.survivorship_notes: These consequences may occur despite treatment that successfully resolves the erection. Erectile recovery after shunt surgery is related to episode duration, pre-operative erectile status and age.

conditions.name: malignant priapism
conditions.description: A rare form of priapism resulting from metastatic or regional tumour infiltration; bladder and prostate are more frequent primary sites.
conditions.epidemiology: In a retrospective study of 412 men with ischaemic priapism, eleven (3.5%) had malignant priapism; seven cases involved local invasion, while the remaining cases were attributed to haematological malignancy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An infiltrative malignant process may underlie the priapism. Penile pain may persist despite palliative treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a possible pelvic or genitourinary malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During physical examination for ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate malignant priapism.

conditions.name: Partial priapism
synonyms: idiopathic partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavemosum
conditions.description: A rare form generally classified as priapism affecting a single crus. A thrombus is present within the corpus cavernosum rather than ischaemia.

conditions.name: Stuttering priapism
conditions.description: Repeated painful episodes of prolonged erection resolve spontaneously between events. Episodes resemble ischaemic priapism but are usually shorter; an individual episode can progress to prolonged ischaemic priapism.
conditions.epidemiology: Robust epidemiological studies are lacking. Recurrent episodes occur in 42-64% of men with SCD. Among adolescents and young men, the reported incidence of priapism is 35%, and 72% of those affected have a history of stuttering priapism.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Episodes may occur several times daily or only once every few months, with intervals free of events that can last months or years. They commonly begin during sleep and persist after waking. The penis is painful and rigid during an episode and usually normal between episodes, although fibrosis can occur; enlargement termed megalo-phallus is rare.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the pattern, duration and recurrence of episodes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Repeated prolonged erections separated by detumescence support the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical and sexual history, physical examination, laboratory testing and penile imaging
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the episode and possible underlying causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Using the diagnostic approach described for ischaemic priapism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Painful, rigid episodes resemble ischaemic priapism; findings between episodes may include penile fibrosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism during an acute episode.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As described for the evaluation of ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate priapism subtypes during an acute episode.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As described for the evaluation of ischaemic priapism, before aspiration.

diagnostic_workup.test: Full blood count, white blood cell count with blood cell differential, platelet count and coagulation profile
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify haematological abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As described for the evaluation of ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate sickle cell disease or thalassemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For patients at high risk, following the diagnostic recommendations for ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess smooth-muscle viability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For prolonged or refractory ischaemic episodes, following the diagnostic recommendations for ischaemic priapism.

recommended_tests: History and clinical examination to assess whether treatment prevents or reduces episodes
long_term_effects: Permanent erectile dysfunction after recurrent episodes
Risk of progression to a prolonged ischaemic episode

conditions.name: Priapism in children
conditions.description: Childhood priapism is classified similarly to adult priapism, with neonatal priapism described as an additional type. Untreated ischaemic episodes may have consequences in adulthood.
conditions.epidemiology: It is considered rare, but prevalence data are unavailable. Sickle cell disease is the leading cause, followed by leukaemia (10%), trauma (10%), idiopathic causes (19%) and drugs (5%). One study reported SCD-related priapism before puberty in 25% of children; another found that 90% of men with SCD experienced their first episode before age 20 years.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Presentation depends on the priapism subtype.

subtypes.name: neonatal priapism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as an additional childhood subtype.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the cause of childhood priapism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For all children presenting with priapism.

long_term_effects: Erectile dysfunction in adulthood after untreated ischaemic priapism
Psychosexual disorders in adulthood after untreated ischaemic priapism

conditions.name: Non-ischaemic priapism
conditions.description: A persistent erection caused by unregulated arterial inflow into the corpora. Blunt trauma can produce a fistula between a cavernosal artery or its branches and the sinusoidal spaces.
conditions.epidemiology: It comprises 5% of priapism cases. Epidemiological information comes almost entirely from small case series, and blunt perineal or penile trauma is the most frequent cause.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The corpora are tumescent but usually not fully rigid. Penile pain is generally absent, although discomfort is possible, and rigidity may fluctuate. After trauma, onset may be delayed by several hours to weeks; the guide also describes delays of up to two to three weeks. Sexual stimulation can produce full rigidity, so intercourse is usually possible. Erectile dysfunction or distal penile flaccidity may develop over time.

subtypes.name: traumatic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Associated with injury, especially blunt perineal or penile trauma.

subtypes.name: neurogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May follow acute spinal cord injury.

subtypes.name: iatrogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reported after certain procedures, including shunting for ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis and distinguish the priapism subtype.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A history of pelvic, perineal or genital trauma, little or no penile pain, and a persistent erection without full rigidity support arterial priapism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess tumescence and identify evidence of trauma.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The corpora are generally tumescent without being fully rigid.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible neurogenic cause.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If neurogenic non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: Complete blood count with white blood cell differential and coagulation profile
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anaemia and other haematological abnormalities.

diagnostic_workup.test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The aspirate is bright red and has normal arterial blood gas values; the listed arterial values are pO2 > 90 mmHg, pCO2 < 40 mmHg and pH 7.40.

diagnostic_workup.test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish priapism subtypes and locate an arterial fistula.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation, without intracavernosal vasoactive drug injection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A fistula may appear as a focal colour blush with turbulent, high-velocity flow. Cavernosal arterial velocities are normal to high.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the site of arterial injury for planned embolisation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A characteristic blush may appear at the injury site.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate selected cases or assess distal penile fibrosis during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Its diagnostic role in non-ischaemic priapism is limited; it may be used during close follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Small penile vessels and fistulae are difficult to demonstrate with MRI.

follow_up.schedule: Close follow-up is described during conservative management and after selective arterial embolisation; no fixed interval is specified.
recommended_tests: Colour duplex ultrasound during conservative management
Colour duplex ultrasound and MRI to detect distal penile fibrosis
Clinical examination, colour duplex ultrasound and erectile function assessment after embolisation
Repeat arteriography if findings remain uncertain
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Follow-up assesses treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical and functional consequences.

conditions.name: High-flow priapism in children
conditions.description: A rare childhood form of non-ischaemic priapism. Its causes, clinical features and general diagnostic principles are comparable to those in adults, although idiopathic cases occur in a significant percentage of children.
conditions.epidemiology: The condition is rare in children; reluctance to discuss symptoms with parents may contribute to misdiagnosis and underestimation of its prevalence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Compression of the perineum with a thumb may cause immediate detumescence, with the erection returning when compression is released.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Immediate detumescence followed by return of the erection after release may support non-ischaemic priapism.

diagnostic_workup.test: History, physical examination, blood count with white blood cell differential and coagulation profile
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the subtype and possible cause using principles comparable to those for adults.
Distinguish non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Non-ischaemic priapism has arterial-type blood gas values.

diagnostic_workup.test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate priapism subtypes and identify a fistula.
Assess the arterial lesion before embolisation.

recommendations.statement: Consider hyaluronic acid (HA), poly-l-lactic acid (PLA), hydroxyethyl methacrylate, polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), polyalkylamide hydrogel (PAAG) or calcium hydroxyapatite as injectable materials for penile girth enhancement.
recommendations.context: There is insufficient evidence to favor one treatment over another.
recommendations.rationale: The evidence is limited, although HA, PLA and PMMA have more supporting evidence than the other listed materials.
recommendations.source_heading: There is lack of evidence to recommend one treatment over another.

recommendations.statement: Do not use silicone, paraffin or Vaseline for penile girth enhancement.
recommendations.source_heading: There is lack of evidence to recommend one treatment over another.

recommendations.statement: Obtain a thorough history to establish the diagnosis and help identify the priapism subtype.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Examine the genitalia, perineum and abdomen as part of the diagnostic assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Obtain a full blood count, white blood cell count with blood cell differential, platelet count and coagulation profile. Select additional laboratory tests according to the history and clinical and laboratory findings. In children, assess all possible causes of priapism comprehensively.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Screen for haemoglobinopathies in patients with low flow priapism who have a high risk of sickle cell disease or thalassemia.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Assess blood gas parameters in aspirated penile blood to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Before aspiration, perform colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Use penile magnetic resonance imaging for prolonged or refractory ischaemic priapism and as an additional means of predicting smooth muscle viability.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Begin treatment of ischaemic priapism as soon as possible, within four to six hours, using a stepwise approach.
recommendations.rationale: Urgent treatment aims to prevent irreversible corporal injury and erectile dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: As the initial treatment, aspirate and wash out the corpus cavernosum until fresh red blood is obtained.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: When priapism follows intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents, use an intracavernous sympathomimetic injection instead of blood aspiration as the first treatment step.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: If priapism continues after aspiration, inject a sympathomimetic drug intracavernously.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: If priapism persists after aspiration and an intracavernous sympathomimetic injection, repeat both interventions before considering surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Treat ischaemic priapism associated with sickle cell disease as for idiopathic ischaemic priapism. Do not use exchange transfusion as the primary intervention. Provide supportive measures, including intravenous hydration, oxygen with bicarbonate alkalisation and blood exchange transfusions, without postponing initial penile treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence that exchange transfusion resolves priapism is inconclusive, and serious neurological sequelae have been reported.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Proceed to surgery only if aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetic injections have failed.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Perform a distal shunt first, adding tunnelling when needed.
recommendations.context: Surgical treatment after failed medical management.
recommendations.rationale: Distal shunts are less invasive and have lower reported rates of post-operative erectile dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Use a proximal procedure if a distal shunt fails in priapism lasting < 48 hours, or if the patient does not want immediate penile implant insertion.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Discuss penile prosthesis implantation when presentation is delayed > 48 hours or priapism remains refractory to injection therapy and distal shunting.
recommendations.rationale: Prolonged or refractory ischaemic priapism commonly results in erectile dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: After a shunt has been performed, postpone penile prosthesis implantation to reduce implant infection and erosion risk.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Choose the implant type according to patient suitability, the surgeon’s experience, and equipment availability and cost. A malleable penile prosthesis can subsequently be replaced with an inflatable penile implant.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Treat every acute episode according to the treatment recommendations for ischaemic priapism.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

recommendations.statement: For patients with frequent relapses, use hormonal therapies, mainly gonadotropin-receptor hormone agonists or antagonists, and/or anti-androgens to prevent further episodes. Do not use these therapies before sexual maturation.
recommendations.rationale: Hormonal treatment can cause adverse effects and interfere with sexual maturation and fertility.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

recommendations.statement: Start phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors only while the penis is flaccid.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

recommendations.statement: Restrict digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin and terbutaline to patients whose relapses are frequent and uncontrolled.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence supporting these systemic drugs is limited.

recommendations.statement: Use home intracavernous self-injection of sympathomimetic drugs as a temporary treatment for acute episodes until ischaemic priapism has been alleviated.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

recommendations.statement: Take a comprehensive history to establish the diagnosis and help determine the priapism subtype.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Include examination of the genitalia, perineum and abdomen in the diagnostic assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Perform a neurological examination when a neurogenic cause of non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Obtain a complete blood count with white blood cell differential and a coagulation profile.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Analyse blood gas parameters in aspirated penile blood to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Use colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: Perform selected pudendal arteriography when embolisation is planned for non-ischaemic priapism.

recommendations.statement: Leave the decision to undertake definitive management of non-ischaemic priapism to the treating physician’s discretion.
recommendations.context: The condition is not a medical emergency.

recommendations.statement: Begin with conservative treatment using site-specific perineal compression. Consider androgen deprivation therapy only for adults.

recommendations.statement: Perform selective arterial embolisation if conservative treatment fails.

recommendations.statement: Use temporary material for the first selective arterial embolisation.
recommendations.source_heading: 10.3.3.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism

recommendations.statement: If non-ischaemic priapism recurs after selective arterial embolisation, repeat embolisation using temporary or permanent material.

recommendations.statement: Reserve selective surgical fistula ligation as the final treatment option after repeated arterial embolisation has failed.
