therapies_index.name: Hyaluronic acid (HA)
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement; the supporting evidence is limited.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: poly-l-lactic acid (PLA)
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement; the supporting evidence is limited.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: hydroxyethyl methacrylate
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement, with low-level evidence.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA)
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement; the supporting evidence is limited.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: polyalkylamide hydrogel (PAAG)
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement, with low-level evidence.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: calcium hydroxyapatite
approved_indications: Considered as an injectable material for penile girth enhancement, with low-level evidence.
therapies_index.administration: Penile injection; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: penile lengthening or girth enhancement surgery
key_toxicities: Poor satisfaction, erectile function and sensitivity have been reported in men with normal penis size.

therapies_index.name: dorsal nerve block
approved_indications: An anaesthesia option before interventions for painful ischaemic priapism.

therapies_index.name: circumferential penile block
approved_indications: An anaesthesia option before interventions for painful ischaemic priapism.

therapies_index.name: subcutaneous local penile shaft block
approved_indications: An anaesthesia option before interventions for painful ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous penile shaft block.

therapies_index.name: oral conscious sedation
approved_indications: An option for paediatric patients undergoing treatment for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral.

therapies_index.name: corporal blood aspiration
therapies_index.mechanism: Drains stagnant cavernosal blood and relieves the pressure associated with ischaemic priapism.
approved_indications: First intervention for ischaemic priapism lasting more than 4 hours; repeat it with sympathomimetic injection if the erection persists.
therapies_index.administration: Access a corpus cavernosum through the glans or lateral proximal penile shaft with a 16 or 18 G angio-catheter or butterfly needle; continue aspiration until bright red blood is obtained.
monitoring: Assess detumescence and whether the aspirated blood becomes bright red.

therapies_index.name: 0.9% w/v saline solution
approved_indications: Intracorporeal irrigation alongside aspiration for ischaemic priapism; the added benefit over aspiration alone is uncertain.
therapies_index.administration: Use for cavernosal irrigation with blood aspiration. In a cited RCT, the best reported results followed irrigation with 10°C saline after aspiration.

therapies_index.name: aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines drainage of ischaemic cavernosal blood with pharmacological detumescence.
approved_indications: Described as standard care for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Aspirate cavernosal blood, with or without saline irrigation, and administer an intracavernous sympathomimetic agent.
monitoring: Assess detumescence; monitor blood pressure and pulse during sympathomimetic administration.

therapies_index.name: phenylephrine
therapies_index.mechanism: Selectively activates the α-1-adrenergic receptor without the cardiac β-mediated effects described for other agents.
approved_indications: Preferred adrenergic agonist for ischaemic priapism; also used for temporary home self-injection during acute episodes of stuttering priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous injection of 200 μg every 3-5 minutes; maximum 1 mg within 1 hour. A concentration of 100-500 μg/mL in normal saline is described. Lower doses are recommended for children and patients with severe cardiovascular diseases. Compress the puncture site and massage the corpus cavernosum after injection.
key_toxicities: Potential headache, dizziness, hypertension, reflex bradycardia, tachycardia and palpitations; sporadic subarachnoid haemorrhage is reported for intracavernous sympathomimetics.
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during administration and every fifteen minutes for 1 hour after injection, particularly in older men with cardiovascular disease.

therapies_index.name: etilephrine
therapies_index.mechanism: Directly stimulates adrenergic receptors.
approved_indications: Intracavernous treatment of priapism; oral prevention of recurrent episodes associated with SCD; temporary home self-injection for acute stuttering episodes.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernosal injection at a concentration of 2.5 mg in 1-2 mL normal saline. For recurrence prevention, oral 5-10 mg daily is described.
key_toxicities: Tachycardia and palpitations are reported for oral α-adrenergic agonists.
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous sympathomimetic administration.

therapies_index.name: ephedrine
approved_indications: Studied as medical prophylaxis for stuttering priapism; a cited placebo-controlled study found no efficacy difference compared with etilephrine.
key_toxicities: Tachycardia and palpitations are reported for oral α-adrenergic agonists.

therapies_index.name: epinephrine
approved_indications: Listed among intracavernous sympathomimetic options for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous administration; no agent-specific dose is given.
key_toxicities: Intracavernous sympathomimetics may cause hypertension and other cardiovascular effects.
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous administration.

therapies_index.name: norepinephrine
approved_indications: Listed among intracavernous sympathomimetic options for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous administration; no agent-specific dose is given.
key_toxicities: Intracavernous sympathomimetics may cause hypertension and other cardiovascular effects.
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous administration.

therapies_index.name: metaraminol
approved_indications: Listed among intracavernous sympathomimetic options for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous administration; no agent-specific dose is given.
key_toxicities: Intracavernous sympathomimetics may cause hypertension and other cardiovascular effects.
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous administration.

therapies_index.name: adrenaline
therapies_index.mechanism: Has adrenergic receptor agonist activity.
approved_indications: Described as an intracavernous option for short-term ischaemic priapism following injection of vasoactive agents, on the basis of limited literature.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous injection of 2 mL of 1/100,000 adrenaline solution up to five times over a 20-minute period.

therapies_index.name: Methylene blue
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits guanylate cyclase and may inhibit endothelial-mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle.
approved_indications: Reported in small retrospective series for short-term pharmacologically induced priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Inject 50-100 mg intracavernously, leave for 5 minutes, then aspirate and compress the penis for an additional 5 minutes.
key_toxicities: Transient burning and blue penile discolouration.

therapies_index.name: terbutaline
therapies_index.mechanism: A β-2-agonist with minor β-1 and some α-agonist activity; its action in priapism is not fully understood.
approved_indications: Mainly described for preventing recurrent prolonged erections; studied for priapism following intracavernous injection of erectogenic agents. For stuttering priapism, the recommendation restricts use to frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
therapies_index.administration: Oral 5 mg for priapism lasting more than 2.5 hours after intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents.
key_toxicities: Nervousness, shakiness, drowsiness, palpitations, headache, dizziness, hot flushes, nausea and weakness.

therapies_index.name: salbutamol
therapies_index.mechanism: β-2-agonist.
approved_indications: Studied for prolonged erection after intracavernous injection of erectogenic agents; stronger evidence is needed before oral treatment can be recommended for ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration is discussed without a specified dose.

therapies_index.name: pseudoephedrine
therapies_index.mechanism: Its effect on cavernosal smooth muscle is not fully understood.
approved_indications: Described as a possible first-line oral option for stuttering priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Oral; no dose is specified.
key_toxicities: Tachycardia and palpitations are reported for oral α-adrenergic agonists.

therapies_index.name: intravenous hydration
approved_indications: Supportive treatment for SCD-related priapism while penile aspiration and irrigation are being prepared; it must not delay penile treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Intravenous.

therapies_index.name: narcotic analgesia
approved_indications: Pain control in SCD-related priapism while preparing for aspiration and irrigation.

therapies_index.name: supplemental oxygen administration
approved_indications: A potentially helpful supportive measure for SCD-related priapism that must not delay initial penile treatment.

therapies_index.name: bicarbonate
therapies_index.mechanism: Used for alkalinisation.
approved_indications: A potentially helpful supportive measure for SCD-related priapism that must not delay initial penile treatment.

therapies_index.name: exchange blood transfusion
therapies_index.mechanism: Proposed to increase oxygen delivery to tissues.
approved_indications: Not recommended as routine primary treatment for SCD-related priapism; it may be needed after failed medical treatment to permit safe general anaesthesia before definitive surgery, or in the context of other SCD-related symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: Transfused blood should be sickle cell haemoglobin negative and matched for Rh and Kell antigens.
key_toxicities: Serious neurological sequelae, including reported ASPEN syndrome.

therapies_index.name: acetylsalicylic acid
approved_indications: Included in a peri-procedural anti-thrombotic approach reported to reduce priapism recurrence after shunt surgery.
therapies_index.administration: 325 mg pre-operatively and 81 mg post-operatively for 5 days in the reported approach.

therapies_index.name: heparin
approved_indications: Included in a peri-procedural anti-thrombotic approach reported after shunt surgery; also listed among medications associated with priapism.
therapies_index.administration: 5000 IU intraoperatively in the reported anti-thrombotic approach.

therapies_index.name: clopidogrel
approved_indications: Included in a post-operative anti-thrombotic approach reported after shunt surgery.
therapies_index.administration: 75 mg post-operatively for 5 days in the reported approach.

therapies_index.name: penile shunt surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a route for ischaemic blood to leave the corpus cavernosum and permits restoration of circulation.
approved_indications: Second-line treatment for ischaemic priapism after aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment have failed; distal procedures are preferred as the first surgical approach.
therapies_index.administration: Assess the outcome by penile rigidity or repeat cavernosal blood gas testing.
key_toxicities: Post-operative ED; recovery of erectile function after prolonged priapism is poor.
monitoring: Observe penile rigidity or repeat cavernosal blood gas testing to establish whether the shunt succeeded.

therapies_index.name: Winter’s procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Forms a drainage fistula between the glans and each corpus cavernosum.
approved_indications: Described as a percutaneous distal shunt for refractory ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Create the fistula with a Trucut biopsy needle.
key_toxicities: Reported drainage failure and premature shunt closure; post-operative sequelae are uncommon.

therapies_index.name: Ebbehoj’s technique
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates distal tunical openings between the glans and each corpus cavernosum.
approved_indications: Described as a percutaneous distal shunt for refractory ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Pass a size 11 blade scalpel percutaneously several times to make multiple openings.

therapies_index.name: T-Shunt
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a distal route for drainage of cavernosal blood.
approved_indications: Described as a distal shunt for refractory ischaemic priapism; tunnelling may be added.
therapies_index.administration: Insert a size 10 blade through the glans beside the urethral meatus into the cavernosal tip, rotate it 90° laterally and withdraw it; perform the opposite side if necessary.
key_toxicities: Potential urethral injury during associated tunnelling.

therapies_index.name: tunnelling
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides drainage farther along the corpus cavernosum after a distal shunt.
approved_indications: May be combined with distal shunting; described as necessary when priapism duration is > 48 hours.
therapies_index.administration: Use a size 8/10 Hegar dilator through the glans, or a 7 mm metal sound or 7/8 Hegar dilator as described for prolonged cases. US guidance may help avoid urethral injury.
key_toxicities: Potential urethral injury.

therapies_index.name: Al-Ghorab’s procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Opens the distal tunica albuginea to drain cavernosal blood through the glans.
approved_indications: Described as an open distal shunt for refractory ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Excise bilateral circular cone segments of distal tunica albuginea through the glans and close the glans with absorbable running suture.
key_toxicities: A transverse glans incision may compromise arterial blood flow.

therapies_index.name: Burnett’s technique (Snake manoeuvre)
therapies_index.mechanism: Extends an Al-Ghorab shunt with cavernosal tunnelling and manual blood evacuation.
approved_indications: Described as an open distal approach for refractory ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Introduce a 7/8 Hegar dilator retrogradely through the Al-Ghorab opening into each corpus cavernosum; after withdrawal, compress the penis from proximal to distal and close the glans after detumescence.
key_toxicities: Wound infection, penile skin necrosis and urethrocutaneous fistulae.

therapies_index.name: Quackles’s technique
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a proximal communication between the corpus cavernosum and corpus spongiosum.
approved_indications: Described as a proximal shunt option after distal shunt failure or when immediate implantation is not desired.
therapies_index.administration: Use a trans-scrotal or perineal approach.
key_toxicities: Urethro-cavernous fistula, urethral stricture, cavernositis and higher documented ED rates with proximal shunts.

therapies_index.name: Peno-scrotal decompression
therapies_index.mechanism: Opens the proximal corpus cavernosum and uses proximal and distal tunnelling for decompression while sparing the glans.
approved_indications: Described as a potential technique for refractory priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Open the proximal corpus cavernosum and tunnel in both directions with a suction tip.
key_toxicities: May delay prosthesis insertion, with potential penile shortening and prosthetic infection.

therapies_index.name: Grayhack’s procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates venous drainage from the corpus cavernosum using the saphenous vein.
approved_indications: Described as a venous shunt for refractory ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Mobilise the saphenous vein and anastomose it end-to-side to the corpus cavernosum.
key_toxicities: Saphenofemoral thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

therapies_index.name: penile prosthesis implantation
approved_indications: Consider for delayed or refractory ischaemic priapism, particularly with evidence of cavernosal smooth muscle necrosis or failed shunting; may be considered for severe persistent ED after priapism. For medically refractory stuttering priapism, reserve it as a last resort in carefully selected patients.
therapies_index.administration: For early insertion after ischaemic priapism, the stated optimal interval is within the first three weeks. Implantation can be delayed after a shunt to allow oedema to subside and wounds to heal.
key_toxicities: Infection, distal erosion, revision surgery, penile shortening and potential curvature; delayed insertion in corporal fibrosis is more difficult.

therapies_index.name: malleable penile prosthesis
approved_indications: Recommended as an immediate implant option for delayed or refractory ischaemic priapism to avoid difficulties associated with later corporal fibrosis.
therapies_index.administration: Insert immediately when selected; exchange for an inflatable implant can be undertaken later.
key_toxicities: Prosthetic infection and erosion are potential complications of immediate implantation.

therapies_index.name: inflatable penile prosthesis
approved_indications: May be inserted immediately in appropriately counselled and motivated patients with refractory or delayed ischaemic priapism; can also replace a malleable prosthesis later.
therapies_index.administration: If inserted immediately, begin cycling the device immediately.
key_toxicities: Infection; failure to cycle immediately may permit a fibrous capsule to form and contract, contributing to curvature or shortening.

therapies_index.name: vacuum device
approved_indications: May be used to limit fibrosis and penile shortening while prosthesis insertion is postponed after shunt surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Use during the waiting period before implantation.

therapies_index.name: GnRH agonists or antagonists
therapies_index.mechanism: Lower circulating testosterone to suppress androgen effects on erection.
approved_indications: Hormonal prevention of frequent recurrent episodes of stuttering priapism; they should not be used before sexual maturation.
key_toxicities: Hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido, asthenia, contraceptive effects, interference with sexual maturation and spermatogenesis, and effects on fertility.

therapies_index.name: antiandrogens
therapies_index.mechanism: Suppress androgen-associated mechanisms implicated in recurrent erections.
approved_indications: Prevention of frequent relapses of stuttering priapism; not for use before sexual maturation.
key_toxicities: Hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido, asthenia, infertility and interference with sexual maturation and spermatogenesis.

therapies_index.name: oestrogens
therapies_index.mechanism: Used as hormonal manipulation to reduce circulating testosterone.
approved_indications: Described as a hormonal approach for recurrent priapism, but cardiovascular toxicity limits clinical use.
key_toxicities: Potential cardiovascular toxicity; hormonal approaches may cause hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido and asthenia.

therapies_index.name: 5-α-reductase inhibitors
approved_indications: Described as an alternative endocrine approach used with some success for stuttering priapism.

therapies_index.name: ketoconazole
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces adrenal and testicular androgen production.
approved_indications: Described as an alternative endocrine approach for stuttering priapism and in case reports of fistula closure in non-ischaemic priapism.
key_toxicities: Sexual dysfunction is a consideration with androgen deprivation for non-ischaemic priapism.

therapies_index.name: digoxin
therapies_index.mechanism: Modulates smooth muscle tone through several pathways, promoting penile detumescence.
approved_indications: Described for idiopathic stuttering priapism; the recommendation limits its use to frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
therapies_index.administration: Maintenance doses of 0.25-0.5 mg/daily are described.
key_toxicities: Reduced libido, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion, blurred vision, headache, gynaecomastia, rash and arrhythmia.

therapies_index.name: gabapentin
therapies_index.mechanism: Proposed to inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels, attenuate synaptic transmission and reduce testosterone and FSH levels.
approved_indications: Described for stuttering priapism; the recommendation limits its use to frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
therapies_index.administration: 400 mg four times daily, up to 2,400 mg daily until complete detumescence, followed by 300 mg/daily for maintenance.
key_toxicities: Anorgasmia and impaired erectile function.

therapies_index.name: baclofen
therapies_index.mechanism: Acts through GABA activity to inhibit erection and ejaculation.
approved_indications: Described for recurrent reflexogenic or prolonged erections related to neurological disease; for stuttering priapism, the recommendation limits use to frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
therapies_index.administration: Intrathecal administration is described as more effective than oral treatment, which has little efficacy and is not usually used for stuttering priapism.
key_toxicities: Drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, headache, hypotension and nausea.

therapies_index.name: Hydroxyurea
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, blocking DNA synthesis and arresting cells in the S-phase.
approved_indications: Established treatment to ameliorate SCD; evidence for preventing recurrent priapism is limited.
key_toxicities: Oligozoospermia and leg ulcers.

therapies_index.name: PDE5Is
approved_indications: Low doses are described for alleviating and preventing idiopathic or SCD-associated stuttering priapism; start only when the penis is flaccid, not during an acute episode.
therapies_index.administration: Begin while the penis is flaccid; the described effect begins after one week.
key_toxicities: Sporadic priapism cases have been reported after use, but causation is uncertain because additional risk factors were common.

therapies_index.name: intracavernous self-injections of sympathomimetic drugs
approved_indications: Temporary home treatment of acute stuttering-priapism episodes while systemic preventive treatment has not yet taken effect.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous self-injection at home; phenylephrine and etilephrine are the drugs most commonly described.
key_toxicities: Sympathomimetic agents can cause hypertension and cardiovascular effects.
monitoring: Blood pressure and pulse monitoring is advised for intracavernous sympathomimetic administration.

therapies_index.name: Tissue plasminogen activator (TPA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which has fibrinolytic activity.
approved_indications: A single intracavernous injection has been described for recalcitrant priapism, on the basis of limited clinical data.
therapies_index.administration: Single intracavernous injection; no dose is specified.
key_toxicities: Mild bleeding.

therapies_index.name: ice packs
approved_indications: Historically described for ischaemic priapism, with limited evidence and possible worsening in SCD; perineal ice is also a conservative option in non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Apply to the perineum for conservative management of non-ischaemic priapism.
key_toxicities: Conservative cooling measures may exacerbate priapism in patients with SCD.

therapies_index.name: exercise
approved_indications: Historically described for ischaemic priapism; evidence of benefit is limited and conservative measures may worsen SCD-related episodes.

therapies_index.name: ejaculation
approved_indications: Historically described for ischaemic priapism; evidence of benefit is limited.

therapies_index.name: cold baths
approved_indications: Historically described for ischaemic priapism; evidence of benefit is limited and conservative measures may worsen SCD-related episodes.

therapies_index.name: cold water enemas
approved_indications: Historically described for ischaemic priapism, with limited evidence of benefit.

therapies_index.name: perineal compression
therapies_index.mechanism: Applies pressure at the suspected fistula site in non-ischaemic priapism.
approved_indications: First conservative step for non-ischaemic priapism; may be particularly useful in children.
therapies_index.administration: Apply site-specific pressure, typically with US guidance. Thumb compression is described in children.
monitoring: Physical examination and colour duplex US may be used to assess response.

therapies_index.name: androgen deprivation therapy
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces spontaneous and sleep-related erections, potentially allowing an arterial fistula to close.
approved_indications: May be considered for non-ischaemic priapism only in adults; reported in case series rather than established as the first conservative intervention.
therapies_index.administration: Examples in the guide are leuprolide injections, bicalutamide and ketoconazole; no regimen is specified.
key_toxicities: Sexual dysfunction.

therapies_index.name: leuprolide
approved_indications: Mentioned as an injected example of androgen deprivation used in case series of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Injection; no dose or schedule is specified.
key_toxicities: Sexual dysfunction is a consideration with androgen deprivation therapy.

therapies_index.name: bicalutamide
approved_indications: Mentioned as an example of androgen deprivation used in case series of non-ischaemic priapism.
key_toxicities: Sexual dysfunction is a consideration with androgen deprivation therapy.

therapies_index.name: selective arterial embolisation
therapies_index.mechanism: Occludes the arterial fistula responsible for non-ischaemic priapism.
approved_indications: Recommended after conservative treatment fails; repeat embolisation is an option for recurrence.
therapies_index.administration: The first procedure is recommended with temporary material; repeat procedures may use temporary or permanent material.
key_toxicities: ED, penile gangrene, gluteal ischaemia, cavernositis and perineal abscess.
monitoring: After embolisation, assess clinically, with colour duplex US and erectile function assessment; repeat arteriography if the result remains uncertain.

therapies_index.name: autologous blood clot
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporary material for arterial embolisation.
approved_indications: Described for selective arterial embolisation of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Use as a temporary embolic substance.

therapies_index.name: gel foam
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporary material for arterial embolisation.
approved_indications: Described for selective arterial embolisation of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Use as a temporary embolic substance.

therapies_index.name: microcoils
therapies_index.mechanism: Permanent material for arterial embolisation.
approved_indications: Described for selective arterial embolisation of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Use as a permanent embolic substance.

therapies_index.name: ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer (PVA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Permanent material for arterial embolisation.
approved_indications: Described for selective arterial embolisation of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Use as a permanent embolic substance.

therapies_index.name: N-butyl-cyanoacrylate (NBCA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Permanent material for arterial embolisation.
approved_indications: Described for selective arterial embolisation of non-ischaemic priapism.
therapies_index.administration: Use as a permanent embolic substance.

therapies_index.name: surgical ligation of the fistula
therapies_index.mechanism: Closes the fistula responsible for non-ischaemic priapism.
approved_indications: Final treatment option when repeated embolisation fails; also discussed when embolisation is contraindicated or unavailable, or in selected patients seeking definitive treatment who are not sexually active or already have ED.
therapies_index.administration: A transcorporeal or inguinoscrotal approach with intraoperative Doppler US is described.
key_toxicities: Significant ED risk, with the highest reported ED rates among the treatments discussed for non-ischaemic priapism.

therapies_index.name: palliative penectomy
approved_indications: May be considered for selected patients with malignant priapism when other palliative options do not control penile pain.

therapies_index.name: papaverine
approved_indications: Named as a vasoactive erectile agent; papaverine-based intracavernous combinations are associated with a higher priapism risk.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous use is described without a dose.
key_toxicities: Ischaemic priapism, particularly with papaverine-based combinations.

therapies_index.name: phentolamine
approved_indications: Named as a vasoactive erectile agent.
key_toxicities: Listed among agents associated with priapism.

therapies_index.name: prostaglandin E1/alprostadil
approved_indications: Named as an intracavernous vasoactive erectile agent.
therapies_index.administration: Intracavernous injection is described without a dose.
key_toxicities: Priapism is reported after injection; the guide reports a risk of < 1% after prostaglandin E1 injection.

therapies_index.name: testosterone
key_toxicities: Listed among hormones associated with priapism, while the guide also states that maintaining physiological testosterone levels does not cause priapism.

special_populations.considerations: SCD is the leading cause of childhood priapism and a frequent cause of recurrent episodes. Evidence specific to SCD-related priapism is limited. Acute episodes require prompt penile treatment coordinated with a haematologist, and haemoglobin S (HbS) percentage should be measured. Exchange transfusion has uncertain benefit for detumescence and has been associated with serious neurological complications.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treat acute ischaemic episodes as idiopathic ischaemic priapism without delaying penile intervention. Provide intravenous hydration and narcotic analgesia while preparing for aspiration and irrigation; supplemental oxygen and alkalinisation with bicarbonate may help. Do not use exchange transfusion as primary treatment unless there is a risk of SCD-related symptoms. After failed medical management, transfusion may be needed to permit general anaesthesia before definitive surgery. If transfusion is used, blood should be sickle cell haemoglobin negative and matched for Rh and Kell antigens. Etilephrine has been used to prevent SCD-related stuttering priapism at oral doses of 5-10 mg daily.

special_populations.considerations: Priapism is considered rare in children, although prevalence data are unavailable. SCD is the principal cause, followed by leukaemia (10%), trauma (10%), idiopathic causes (19%) and drugs (5%). Untreated ischaemic priapism may lead to erectile and psychosexual problems in adulthood. Assessment should investigate all possible causes and involve a multidisciplinary team with haematology and paediatric endocrinology expertise.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Evaluate and treat promptly. Use lower doses of intracavernous Phenylephrine than in adults; the document does not specify a paediatric dose. Oral conscious sedation is an option for penile procedures in paediatric patients.

special_populations.considerations: This presentation is particularly uncommon in children and may be missed if they are reluctant to discuss it with their parents. Idiopathic cases occur. Thumb pressure on the perineum may cause immediate detumescence, with erection returning when pressure is released, and can help distinguish non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Ice applied to the perineum or targeted perineal compression may succeed. Embolisation is technically challenging in children and requires a specialist paediatric vascular radiology department. Consider androgen deprivation therapy only in adults.

special_populations.population: Pre-pubertal boys and adolescents with stuttering priapism
special_populations.considerations: Hormonal treatment can interfere with sexual maturation, spermatogenesis and fertility. Specialist advice from a paediatric endocrinologist is advised when hormonal treatment is being considered.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use hormonal therapies for prevention of recurrent episodes before sexual maturation. Exercise strong caution when prescribing hormonal treatment to pre-pubertal boys and adolescents.

special_populations.population: Men with stuttering priapism who are trying to conceive with their partner
special_populations.considerations: Hormonal agents have contraceptive effects and may impair spermatogenesis and fertility.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Provide comprehensive counselling before hormonal treatment. Sperm cryopreservation may be considered to mitigate potential fertility effects of anti-androgen therapy.

special_populations.population: Patients with cardiovascular disease, significant hypertension or cerebrovascular disease
special_populations.considerations: Intracavernous sympathomimetic agents can raise blood pressure and cause cardiovascular or neurological complications. Monitoring is particularly important in older men with pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use lower doses of Phenylephrine in patients with severe cardiovascular diseases. Monitor pulse and blood pressure during sympathomimetic administration; after Phenylephrine injection, monitor every fifteen minutes for 1 hour. Use Phenylephrine cautiously in men with cardiovascular disease. The management algorithm states that it is contraindicated with a history of cerebro-vascular disease or significant hypertension; the text also identifies malignant or poorly controlled hypertension as a contraindication to intracavernous sympathomimetic agents.

special_populations.considerations: Concomitant sympathomimetic treatment may precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not administer intracavernous sympathomimetic agents together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors.

special_populations.considerations: Priapism caused by regional or metastatic tumour infiltration is rare, and conventional pharmacological treatment is unlikely to work. Bladder and prostate are the more frequent primary cancer sites described.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Obtain penile MRI and offer supportive care and treatment of the primary cancer. Palliative penectomy may be considered in selected patients whose penile pain remains uncontrolled despite palliative options.

special_populations.population: Patients with permanent erectile dysfunction after stuttering priapism
special_populations.considerations: Medical treatment of erectile dysfunction may trigger another ischaemic episode.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use medical treatments for erectile dysfunction cautiously; penile prosthesis implantation can be considered.

special_populations.population: Patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) and severe erectile dysfunction after ischaemic priapism
special_populations.considerations: PDE5Is and intracavernous injections may provoke another priapism episode.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Penile prosthesis implantation is occasionally indicated when severe erectile dysfunction is present and other treatment options are avoided because of recurrence risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men seeking treatment for a perceived or genuine short penis.
decision_rules: Select treatment according to the cause of the complaint and use a multidisciplinary approach that includes medical and ethical considerations.
Refer patients with detected psychopathological symptoms for further medical diagnosis.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Most reported treatment outcomes rest on limited evidence. Findings for penile augmentation are mixed, and the document does not establish one treatment as preferable to another.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men considering injectable materials to increase penile girth.
decision_rules: Discuss the limited evidence for injectable augmentation; HA, PLA and PMMA have more supporting evidence than the other materials listed.

alternative_regimens.name: Hyaluronic acid (HA)
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Evidence remains low, although HA is among the materials with more supporting evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: poly-l-lactic acid (PLA)
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Evidence remains low, although PLA is among the materials with more supporting evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA)
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Evidence remains low, although PMMA is among the materials with more supporting evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: hydroxyethyl methacrylate
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The supporting evidence is low.

alternative_regimens.name: polyalkylamide hydrogel (PAAG)
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The supporting evidence is low.

alternative_regimens.name: calcium hydroxyapatite
alternative_regimens.summary: An injectable material considered for increasing penile girth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The supporting evidence is low.

not_recommended.name: silicone
not_recommended.reason: Its use is opposed with Strong evidence against.

not_recommended.name: paraffin
not_recommended.reason: Its use is opposed with Strong evidence against.

not_recommended.name: Vaseline
not_recommended.reason: Its use is opposed with Strong evidence against.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Fillers have been associated with better genital self-image and self-esteem and fewer PDD symptoms, but no effect was found on self-confidence or satisfaction with sexual relationships.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with acute ischaemic priapism, particularly an erection lasting more than 4 hours.
decision_rules: Begin emergency, stepwise treatment as soon as possible, within four to six hours.
For an episode lasting more than 4 hours, initially decompress the corpora by aspiration and washout until fresh red blood is obtained.
If priapism persists, inject an intracavernous sympathomimetic drug; repeat aspiration and sympathomimetic injection if necessary before proceeding to surgery.
Beyond 48 hours, first-line measures may relieve erection and pain but have little documented benefit for preserving long-term erectile function.

recommended_regimens.name: Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution
recommended_regimens.summary: Drain corporal blood, with washout, as the initial decompression step; continue until bright red blood is obtained. Access may be through the glans or the lateral proximal shaft using a 16 or 18 G catheter or butterfly needle. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether adding saline irrigation improves on aspiration alone.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported success for first-line approaches in case series and retrospective studies ranged from 0 to 100% of cases, but aspiration and irrigation were usually combined with sympathomimetic injection. An RCT involving 70 patients with injection-related ischaemic priapism lasting more than 6 hours reported 85% success with aspiration and saline irrigation at different temperatures; its best results used 10°C saline after aspiration.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Continue aspiration until bright red, oxygenated blood appears.

recommended_regimens.name: Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents
recommended_regimens.summary: Use intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment when aspiration does not resolve priapism; repeat aspiration and injection before surgery if the first combination fails.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported resolution with a sympathomimetic after prior aspiration or irrigation ranged from 80 to 100% of cases, compared with 58% after sympathomimetic injection alone. The evidence summary reports over 80% success for combined treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Phenylephrine
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as the preferred intracavernous adrenergic agonist when sympathomimetic injection is needed. Compress the puncture site and massage the corpus cavernosum after injection.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Intracavernous injection of 200 μg every 3-5 minutes; maximum dosage is 1 mg within 1 hour. The evidence summary describes dilution in normal saline to 100-500 μg/mL.

alternative_regimens.name: Etilephrine
alternative_regimens.summary: An intracavernosal sympathomimetic option described for priapism treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Intracavernosal injection at a concentration of 2.5 mg in 1-2 mL normal saline.

alternative_regimens.name: Methylene blue
alternative_regimens.summary: Small retrospective case series report successful use for short-term pharmacologically-induced priapism.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Intracavernous injection of 50-100 mg, retained for 5 minutes, followed by aspiration and penile compression for an additional 5 minutes.

alternative_regimens.name: Adrenaline
alternative_regimens.summary: Limited reports describe intracavernous use for short-term priapism after injection of vasoactive agents.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Intracavernous injection of 2 mL of 1/100,000 adrenaline solution up to five times over a 20-minute period.

alternative_regimens.name: Terbutaline
alternative_regimens.summary: Oral treatment has been studied for priapism associated with intracavernous injection of erectogenic agents; it does not replace the specified emergency decompression sequence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Oral administration of 5 mg for priapism lasting more than 2.5 hours after intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents. Use cautiously with coronary artery disease, increased intravascular fluid volume, oedema or hypokalaemia.

not_recommended.name: salbutamol
not_recommended.reason: More robust evidence is required before oral salbutamol can be recommended for ischaemic priapism.

not_recommended.name: Intracavernous sympathomimetic agents in malignant or poorly controlled hypertension
not_recommended.reason: These agents can cause hypertension, and significant cardiovascular and neurological complications have been reported.

not_recommended.name: Intracavernous sympathomimetic agents with monoamine oxidase inhibitors
not_recommended.reason: Available data suggest that the combination can cause a hypertensive crisis.

response_assessment.method: Assess detumescence, pain and whether aspiration yields fresh red blood.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent corporal rigidity or cavernosal acidosis, anoxia or severe glucopenia suggests treatment failure; absent cavernosal arterial inflow or raised intracorporal pressure provides further evidence of failure.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every fifteen minutes for 1 hour after Phenylephrine injection
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for cardiovascular adverse effects, particularly in older men with pre-existing cardiovascular disease.

supportive_care: For severe penile pain, consider a dorsal nerve block, circumferential penile block or subcutaneous local penile shaft block; oral conscious sedation is an option for paediatric patients.
Monitor pulse and blood pressure during intracavernous sympathomimetic administration and for one hour afterwards.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lower Phenylephrine doses are recommended in children and patients with severe cardiovascular diseases. The management algorithm states that Phenylephrine is contraindicated with a history of cerebro-vascular disease or significant hypertension. Exercise, ejaculation, ice packs, cold baths and cold water enemas have limited supporting evidence and may worsen the condition in patients with SCD.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose priapism follows intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents.
decision_rules: For this injection-related presentation, use intracavernous sympathomimetic injection instead of blood aspiration as the initial treatment step.
If the erection persists, follow the subsequent stepwise approach for ischaemic priapism.

recommended_regimens.name: Intracavernous injection of a sympathomimetic drug
recommended_regimens.summary: Use sympathomimetic injection first rather than starting with corporal blood aspiration when the episode was caused by intracavernous vasoactive treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Terbutaline
alternative_regimens.summary: Oral treatment has shown detumescence in studies of injection-associated priapism.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The dosing table specifies 5 mg orally when priapism lasts more than 2.5 hours following intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents.

response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent priapism requires further treatment according to the stepwise ischaemic-priapism pathway.

supportive_care: Monitor blood pressure and pulse during intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence summary reports success with oral terbutaline in up to 60% of injection-associated cases; this figure is not an outcome of intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with acute priapism associated with sickle cell disease (SCD).
decision_rules: Treat the penile episode with the same urgent sequence used for idiopathic ischaemic priapism, without delaying penile treatment for systemic supportive measures.
Coordinate care with a haematologist and measure Haemoglobin S (HbS) percentage.

recommended_regimens.name: Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the acute ischaemic-priapism approach for SCD-associated episodes, including penile aspiration, irrigation and intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment as indicated.

not_recommended.name: exchange transfusion as a primary treatment
not_recommended.reason: Evidence that exchange transfusion itself resolves priapism is inconclusive, and serious neurological sequelae have been reported; routine primary use is not recommended unless there is a risk of SCD-related symptoms.

response_assessment.method: Assess penile detumescence and response to the standard ischaemic-priapism interventions.
response_assessment.interpretation: Failure of medical management may necessitate definitive surgery.

supportive_care: Provide intravenous hydration and narcotic analgesia while preparing for aspiration and irrigation.
Supplemental oxygen and alkalinisation with bicarbonate can be helpful.

If medical management fails, transfusion may be required to permit safe general anaesthesia before definitive surgery; transfused blood should be sickle cell haemoglobin negative and matched for Rh and Kell antigens.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A systematic review found mean time to detumescence of eleven days with exchange transfusions versus eight days with conventional treatment and reported 9 cases of ASPEN syndrome after transfusion. The document characterises the SCD-specific evidence as insufficient for high-quality recommendations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with malignant priapism caused by metastatic or regional tumour infiltration.
decision_rules: Offer supportive care and medical treatment for the primary cancer; conventional pharmacological priapism treatments are unlikely to work.
Consider palliative penectomy in selected patients whose penile pain remains uncontrolled despite other palliative options.

recommended_regimens.name: supportive care and medical intervention for primary cancer
recommended_regimens.summary: Address symptoms and the underlying malignancy rather than relying on conventional pharmacological treatment of priapism.

alternative_regimens.name: palliative penectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible intervention for persistent penile pain.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected cases in which other palliative treatments have not controlled pain.

response_assessment.interpretation: Used to evaluate men with this presentation.
Failure of palliative options to control pain may support consideration of palliative penectomy.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The tumour process often originates in the bladder or prostate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistent ischaemic priapism after aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetic treatment, particularly when presentation is within < 48 hours.
decision_rules: Proceed to surgery only after aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetic injection have failed; at least 1 hour of unsuccessful first-line treatment can be considered before surgery.
Choose a distal shunt as the initial surgical approach and add tunnelling when necessary.
Use a proximal procedure after distal-shunt failure in cases lasting < 48 hours, or when a patient does not want immediate penile implant insertion.
The evidence does not establish superiority among individual shunt techniques.

recommended_regimens.name: distal shunt surgical procedures
recommended_regimens.summary: Create distal drainage from the corpus cavernosum after medical treatment fails; combine with tunnelling when needed. Distal procedures are less invasive and have lower reported postoperative ED rates than proximal approaches.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: When ischaemic priapism resolved within 24 hours, reported recovery of spontaneous functional erections was 78-100%; reports involving priapism lasting more than 36-48 hours found ED > 90%. These outcomes relate to episode duration rather than a proven advantage of any individual shunt.

alternative_regimens.name: Winter’s procedure
alternative_regimens.summary: A percutaneous distal shunt formed between the glans and each corpus cavernosum with a Trucut biopsy needle; it has been reported as the least successful distal-shunt operation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice among shunt techniques depends on surgeon preference and familiarity.

alternative_regimens.name: Ebbehoj’s technique
alternative_regimens.summary: A percutaneous distal shunt using multiple tunical openings between the glans and each corpus cavernosum.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice among shunt techniques depends on surgeon preference and familiarity.

alternative_regimens.name: T-Shunt
alternative_regimens.summary: A distal shunt that may be repeated on the opposite side if the first side fails and may be followed by tunnelling.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider tunnelling when needed; the document states that tunnelling is necessary when priapism duration is > 48 hours.

alternative_regimens.name: Al-Ghorab’s procedure
alternative_regimens.summary: An open distal corpora-glanular shunt involving bilateral excision of distal tunica albuginea tissue.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice among distal techniques depends on surgeon preference and familiarity.

alternative_regimens.name: Burnett’s technique (Snake manoeuvre)
alternative_regimens.summary: A modification of the Al-Ghorab shunt using retrograde corporal dilatation and manual evacuation of blood.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice among distal techniques depends on surgeon preference and familiarity.

alternative_regimens.name: Quackles’s technique
alternative_regimens.summary: An open proximal corpora-spongiosal shunt; proximal procedures are more invasive and have higher documented ED rates.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider a proximal procedure following distal-shunt failure at < 48 hours or when immediate penile implantation is declined.

alternative_regimens.name: Peno-scrotal decompression
alternative_regimens.summary: A glans-sparing proximal decompression approach with proximal and distal tunnelling, described for refractory cases.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Its use may postpone prosthesis implantation and adversely affect subsequent surgical outcomes.

alternative_regimens.name: Grayhack’s procedure
alternative_regimens.summary: A venous shunt connecting a mobilised saphenous vein to the corpus cavernosum.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Technique selection depends on surgeon preference and familiarity; reported complications include saphenofemoral thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

response_assessment.method: Directly assess penile rigidity or repeat testing such as cavernous blood gas analysis.
response_assessment.interpretation: Penile colour US may be misleading during post-decompression hyperaemia.

supportive_care: Peri-operative anticoagulation is advocated to facilitate resolution after shunting. A study reported an 84% decrease in recurrence in the shunt group receiving peri-procedural anti-thrombotic treatment compared with the group without it after failed aspiration; the described treatment was 325 mg acetylsalicylic acid pre-operatively, 5000 IU intraoperative heparin, then 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid and 75 mg clopidogrel post-operatively for 5 days.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Outcomes after shunting depend on priapism duration, pre-operative erectile status and age. Shunting after 36-48 hours may relieve pain without improving erectile function; early prosthesis insertion can instead be considered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men presenting after > 48 hours, with therapy-resistant acute priapism, corporal smooth muscle necrosis, failed shunting or other refractory disease.
decision_rules: Discuss penile prosthesis implantation for presentation after > 48 hours or for disease refractory to injection treatment and distal shunting.
Consider implantation before shunt surgery in delayed cases; MRI or corporal biopsy evidence of smooth muscle necrosis can inform the choice.
When a shunt has already been performed, delay prosthesis implantation to reduce infection and erosion risks.
Choose the implant type according to patient suitability, surgeon experience, and equipment availability and cost.

recommended_regimens.name: penile prosthesis implantation
recommended_regimens.summary: Discuss early insertion for delayed or refractory ischaemic priapism, including failed shunting or documented corporal smooth muscle necrosis. The document recommends immediate insertion of a malleable penile prosthesis to avoid the difficulties of later implantation with fibrosis.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Compared with late insertion, early implantation was associated with infection rates of 6-7% vs. 19-30%, penile shortening of 3% vs. 40%, revision rates of 9% vs. 27%, and satisfaction of 96% vs. 60%.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The stated optimal implantation window is within the first three weeks from the priapism episode; delay implantation if a shunt has been performed.

alternative_regimens.name: inflatable penile prosthesis
alternative_regimens.summary: Immediate insertion may be undertaken in well-motivated patients who have received counselling; a previously inserted malleable implant can also be exchanged for an inflatable device later.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider suitability, surgeon experience and equipment factors. If placed immediately, the device must be cycled immediately to avoid formation and contraction of a fibrous capsule.

alternative_regimens.name: vacuum device
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used to limit fibrosis and shortening while prosthesis implantation is deferred after shunt surgery.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: During the waiting period after a shunt.

response_assessment.timepoint: When delayed or refractory priapism is being evaluated for implantation
response_assessment.method: Gadolinium-enhanced penile MRI or cavernosal smooth muscle biopsy.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evidence of smooth muscle necrosis suggests that shunting is likely to fail and can inform counselling and the implantation decision.

supportive_care: Counsel patients about implant options and the possibility of later exchange from a malleable to an inflatable device.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that clear indications for immediate implantation are not established. A semi-rigid implant is more suitable in most cases because insertion is easier and operative time is shorter. No randomised trials compare malleable and inflatable devices in this setting.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with persistent ED, severe corporal fibrosis or complex penile deformity following ischaemic priapism.
decision_rules: Consider penile prosthesis implantation for severe post-priapism ED.
Adapt implant selection or operative technique when fibrosis, tissue loss or deformity makes standard insertion difficult.

recommended_regimens.name: penile prosthesis implantation
recommended_regimens.summary: A possible treatment for severe ED after ischaemic priapism; narrow-based devices are preferable in severe corporal fibrosis because insertion requires less dilatation.

alternative_regimens.name: penile reconstruction using grafts
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used when severe priapism has caused complicated deformity or tissue loss and concomitant prosthesis implantation is considered.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Complex post-priapism penile destruction or deformity.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In patients with SCD and severe ED, PDE5Is and intracavernous injections are avoided because they may provoke another priapism event. Operative adaptations described for severe fibrosis include multiple corporotomies, corporal excavation, optical corporotomy-Shaeer technique, dilatation with Carrion-Rosello cavernotome, Uramix or Mooreville cavernotome, scar excision and use of a small-diameter prosthesis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients experiencing an acute painful episode of recurrent priapism.
decision_rules: Treat each acute episode according to the recommendations for ischaemic priapism.
Use aspiration and irrigation with intracavernous α-adrenergic agonist injection as indicated.

recommended_regimens.name: Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents
recommended_regimens.summary: Apply the acute ischaemic-priapism treatment sequence to an episode of stuttering priapism.

response_assessment.timepoint: After treatment of an acute episode
response_assessment.method: Assess detumescence and whether the erection progresses to prolonged ischaemic priapism.
response_assessment.interpretation: An episode that does not resolve requires ongoing acute ischaemic-priapism management.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The preventive aim of longer-term treatment is to limit further episodes and progression to prolonged, treatment-resistant ischaemic priapism.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with frequent relapses who have reached sexual maturation.
decision_rules: Use hormonal treatment and/or anti-androgens to prevent further episodes in patients with frequent relapses.
Do not use these treatments before sexual maturation.
Counsel patients attempting conception about effects on fertility; sperm cryopreservation may be considered.

recommended_regimens.name: GnRH agonists or antagonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Reduce circulating testosterone to prevent recurrent episodes in sexually mature patients with frequent relapses.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The document cannot establish an effective dose or treatment duration.

recommended_regimens.name: anti-androgens
recommended_regimens.summary: An option, alone or with hormonal therapies, for prevention of frequent recurrent episodes after sexual maturation.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The document cannot establish an effective dose or treatment duration.

alternative_regimens.name: 5-α-reductase inhibitors
alternative_regimens.summary: An endocrine approach reported to have some success.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The document does not specify when to prefer this approach.

alternative_regimens.name: ketoconazole
alternative_regimens.summary: An endocrine approach reported to have some success.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The document does not specify when to prefer this approach.

not_recommended.name: hormonal therapies before sexual maturation
not_recommended.reason: The recommendation explicitly excludes their use before sexual maturation; hormonal treatment can interfere with sexual maturation, spermatogenesis and fertility.

response_assessment.method: Use history and clinical examination to assess recurrence, erectile function and penile fibrosis.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether treatment prevents or reduces erectile episodes.

supportive_care: Seek specialist paediatric endocrinology advice when hormonal treatment is being considered for pre-pubertal boys or adolescents.
Provide comprehensive fertility counselling to men planning conception with a partner; consider sperm cryopreservation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported adverse effects include hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido, asthenia and infertility. Potential cardiovascular toxicity limits the clinical use of oestrogens.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with idiopathic or SCD-associated recurrent priapism who are between acute episodes.
decision_rules: Start PDE5Is only when the penis is flaccid, never during an acute episode.
Allow for a delay of one week before an effect is expected.

recommended_regimens.name: PDE5Is
recommended_regimens.summary: Low-dose treatment may alleviate and prevent recurrent priapism, mainly in idiopathic and SCD-associated cases; initiation is restricted to the flaccid state.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: A delay of one week precedes treatment effect.

not_recommended.name: PDE5Is during an acute episode
not_recommended.reason: Treatment must begin only when the penis is flaccid.

response_assessment.method: Assess episode frequency or relief, erectile function and penile fibrosis by history and examination.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether recurrent episodes are being prevented or alleviated.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No impairment of male sexual function was reported with this preventive approach.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
decision_rules: Restrict digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin or terbutaline to patients with frequent, uncontrolled relapses.
Consider the limited evidence for these systemic drugs and their differing adverse effects.

recommended_regimens.name: digoxin
recommended_regimens.summary: A systemic option for frequent, uncontrolled recurrence; maintenance use in idiopathic cases has been associated with fewer hospital visits and better QoL.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Maintenance doses of 0.25-0.5 mg/daily are described.

recommended_regimens.name: α-adrenergic agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Oral prophylactic agents for frequent, uncontrolled relapses; the document identifies Pseudoephedrine as a possible first-line option and describes Etilephrine use in SCD-associated recurrence.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported response rates with oral Etilephrine were up to 72%; one placebo-controlled RCT found no efficacy difference between etilephrine and ephedrine.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Etilephrine is usually taken orally at 5-10 mg daily.

recommended_regimens.name: baclofen
recommended_regimens.summary: A restricted option for frequent, uncontrolled recurrence; oral treatment has little efficacy, whereas intrathecal administration is more effective.

recommended_regimens.name: gabapentin
recommended_regimens.summary: A systemic option restricted to frequent, uncontrolled recurrence.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 400 mg, four times daily, up to 2,400 mg daily until complete penile detumescence, followed by maintenance at 300 mg/daily.

recommended_regimens.name: terbutaline
recommended_regimens.summary: A systemic option restricted to frequent, uncontrolled recurrence; the cited detumescence studies involved pharmacologically-induced priapism.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited RCT (n = 68) reported detumescence in 42% of the terbutaline-treated group versus 15% of the placebo-treated group; another reported rate was 36% in alprostadil-induced priapism.

alternative_regimens.name: Hydroxyurea
alternative_regimens.summary: An established treatment for SCD, but evidence for preventing recurrent priapism is limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The document does not establish it as a preferred preventive treatment for recurrent priapism.

response_assessment.method: Use history and clinical examination to assess recurrent episodes, erectile function and penile fibrosis.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether the selected treatment prevents or alleviates episodes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence for digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin, terbutaline and hydroxyurea is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients beginning systemic recurrence-prevention treatment who do not yet have a therapeutic response and develop acute episodes.
decision_rules: Use home intracavernous sympathomimetic self-injection temporarily to treat acute episodes while awaiting benefit from systemic prevention.

recommended_regimens.name: intracavernous self-injections of sympathomimetic drugs
recommended_regimens.summary: Temporary home treatment of acute recurrent episodes; phenylephrine and etilephrine are the drugs most commonly described.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Interim use while systemic treatment has not yet provided benefit.

response_assessment.method: Assess relief of acute erections and response to systemic prevention.
response_assessment.interpretation: Ongoing or prolonged ischaemic priapism requires management according to the acute ischaemic-priapism recommendations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Carefully selected patients with medically refractory recurrent priapism or permanent ED resulting from stuttering priapism.
decision_rules: Consider a penile prosthesis only as a last resort after medical treatment for prevention of recurrent episodes.
For permanent ED, use medical ED treatments cautiously because they may provoke an ischaemic episode; a prosthesis can be considered.

alternative_regimens.name: penile prosthesis
alternative_regimens.summary: May prevent a major ischaemic episode in medically refractory recurrent disease or address permanent ED.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Reserve for carefully selected patients after medical treatment, or consider for permanent ED.

not_recommended.name: penile prosthesis before medical treatment
not_recommended.reason: A prosthesis for prevention of stuttering priapism should be offered only as a last resort after medical therapy.

response_assessment.method: Assess recurrent episodes, erectile function and penile fibrosis through history and clinical examination.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate symptom control and longer-term function.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Patients with medically refractory stuttering priapism may require frequent emergency visits and remain at risk of a major ischaemic episode.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with non-ischaemic priapism, including those with a post-traumatic arterial fistula.
decision_rules: Begin with conservative management using site-specific perineal compression.
Discuss the timing and risks of definitive intervention with the patient; this condition is not classified as a medical emergency, although erectile function may worsen over time.
Consider androgen deprivation therapy only for adults.

recommended_regimens.name: site-specific perineal compression
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as the initial conservative treatment; compression is typically guided by US.

alternative_regimens.name: ice to the perineum
alternative_regimens.summary: A conservative measure described for non-ischaemic priapism.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be used during conservative management.

alternative_regimens.name: androgen deprivation therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Case series describe possible fistula closure through reduction of spontaneous and sleep-related erections; reported agents include leuprolide injections, bicalutamide and ketoconazole.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider only in adults, accounting for possible sexual dysfunction.

not_recommended.name: α-adrenergic antagonists
not_recommended.reason: The document advises against their use because systemic transfer of the drug can cause severe adverse effects.

response_assessment.method: Physical examination and colour duplex US; close follow-up may also include MRI.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess fistula response and detect distal penile fibrosis; findings may support earlier embolisation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Blood aspiration is not helpful as treatment for arterial priapism. A fistula may close spontaneously, but patients can develop ED or distal penile flaccidity during observation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose non-ischaemic priapism persists despite conservative treatment.
decision_rules: Perform selective arterial embolisation when conservative care fails.
Use a temporary material for the first selective embolisation.
Do not presume that temporary material better preserves erectile function or causes more recurrence: the document finds insufficient evidence for that comparison.

recommended_regimens.name: selective arterial embolisation
recommended_regimens.summary: Occlude the responsible artery after conservative treatment fails; the first procedure should use temporary material, such as autologous blood clot or gel foam.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported success after the first arterial embolization ranged between 61.7 and 83.3%, with ED rates from 0-33.3%; these ranges do not establish which material is preferable.

response_assessment.method: Clinical examination, colour duplex US and erectile function assessment; repeat arteriography if findings remain uncertain.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical or functional sequelae.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No optimal interval between conservative care and embolisation is established. Potential embolisation complications include penile gangrene, gluteal ischaemia, cavernositis and perineal abscess.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with recurrent non-ischaemic priapism after selective arterial embolisation.
decision_rules: Repeat selective arterial embolisation for recurrence after an initial embolisation; either temporary or permanent material can be used.

recommended_regimens.name: selective arterial embolisation
recommended_regimens.summary: Repeat the procedure using temporary material, such as autologous blood clot or gel foam, or permanent material, such as microcoils, ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer (PVA) or N-butyl-cyanoacrylate (NBCA).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Repeat for recurrence following prior selective arterial embolisation.

response_assessment.method: Clinical examination, colour duplex US and erectile function assessment; repeat arteriography if needed.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess resolution, further recurrence and anatomical or functional effects.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence does not establish a best temporary or permanent embolic substance for either success or preservation of sexual function.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom selective embolisation is contraindicated or unavailable, or whose repeated embolisations have failed.
decision_rules: Reserve selective surgical fistula ligation as the final treatment option after failed repeat arterial embolisation.
Surgery may also be appropriate when embolisation cannot be used, particularly if a patient seeking definitive treatment is not sexually active or already has ED.

recommended_regimens.name: selective surgical ligation of a fistula
recommended_regimens.summary: A final-option procedure that can use a transcorporeal or inguinoscrotal approach with intraoperative Doppler US.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported ED rates after treatment for non-ischaemic priapism ranged from 0-50%, with surgical ligation having the highest reported rates.

response_assessment.method: Assess erectile function and anatomical or functional sequelae.
response_assessment.interpretation: Long-term ED may lead to consideration of penile prosthesis implantation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Surgical ligation is technically challenging and carries a substantial risk of ED.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with high-flow priapism.
decision_rules: Apply the diagnostic and treatment principles used for arterial priapism in adults, while accounting for paediatric differences.
Try conservative treatment with ice to the perineum or site-specific perineal compression.
If embolisation is required, arrange treatment within a specialist paediatric vascular radiology department.

recommended_regimens.name: site-specific perineal compression
recommended_regimens.summary: A conservative treatment that may be particularly successful in children.

alternative_regimens.name: ice to the perineum
alternative_regimens.summary: A conservative measure that may succeed in children.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: During initial conservative management.

alternative_regimens.name: selective arterial embolisation
alternative_regimens.summary: Reported to be successful but technically challenging in children.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: If intervention is needed after conservative management, use a specialist paediatric vascular radiology department.

not_recommended.name: androgen deprivation therapy in children
not_recommended.reason: The recommendation to consider androgen deprivation therapy for non-ischaemic priapism is limited to adults.

response_assessment.method: Apply thumb compression to the perineum.
response_assessment.interpretation: Immediate detumescence followed by return of the erection after compression is released may help distinguish non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Embarrassment may delay a child's disclosure of symptoms. Idiopathic non-ischaemic priapism is also described in children.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with priapism, particularly those with ischaemic disease or SCD.
decision_rules: Evaluate and treat promptly, following the pathway appropriate to the identified priapism subtype.
Assess possible causes comprehensively and involve a multidisciplinary team, including haematology and paediatric endocrinology expertise.
supportive_care: Use multidisciplinary care with specialist input from haematologists and paediatric endocrinologists.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Untreated childhood ischaemic priapism may result in ED and psychosexual disorders in adulthood. The document describes neonatal priapism as an additional paediatric subtype but provides no separate treatment regimen for it.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence on the epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.1.1.1 Summary of evidence on the epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology of ischaemic priapism

rows: Ischaemic priapism is the most common type, accounting for more than 95% of all cases.
Ischaemic priapism is identified as idiopathic in most patients, while sickle cell disease is the most common cause in childhood.
Ischaemic priapism occurs relatively often (about 5%) after intracavernous injections of papaverinebased combinations, while it is rare (< 1%) after prostaglandin E1 monotherapy.
Priapism is rare in men who have taken PDE5Is, with only sporadic cases reported.
