artifacts.title: Figure 10.1: Differential diagnosis of priapism
artifacts.description: Step 1: Identify a prolonged erection lasting > 4 hours. Step 2: Assess the history: a painful, rigid erection points toward ischaemic priapism; perineal or penile trauma with a painless erection of fluctuating rigidity points toward non-ischaemic priapism. Step 3: Compare penile blood and blood-gas findings: dark blood with hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis supports the ischaemic pathway; bright red blood with arterial blood-gas values supports the non-ischaemic pathway. Step 4: Use penile Doppler US: sluggish or absent flow supports the ischaemic pathway, whereas normal arterial flow with possible turbulent flow at a fistula supports the non-ischaemic pathway.
artifacts.summary: Organises history, corporal blood findings and Doppler US findings into a differential diagnosis of the two principal priapism subtypes.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Subtype identification is necessary because ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism have different treatment pathways.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

rows: Medical history including the assessment of known haematological abnormalities (e.g., SCD), history of pelvic/perineal/genital trauma, prior drug treatment or recreational drug use is essential to identify the possible etiology and the type of priapism.

Blood gas analysis performed before blood aspiration from the corpora is able to differentiate between ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism. Full blood count and haemoglobinopathy screen could reveal haematological alterations.
Penile Colour Doppler US can differentiate from ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism when performed before corporal blood aspiration.
Penile MRI is able to predict non-viable smooth muscle in patients with ischaemic priapism.

artifacts.description: The blood-gas statement refers to analysis before corporal blood aspiration, whereas the diagnostic recommendations in this section specify analysis of blood aspirated from the penis. The table and recommendations differ on this point.
artifacts.summary: Lists the stated evidence levels for history, laboratory testing and imaging in the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Indicates the evidence attached to tests used for subtype differentiation and assessment of smooth-muscle viability.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism

rows: Take a comprehensive history to establish the diagnosis which can help to determine the priapism subtype.
Include a physical examination of the genitalia, perineum and abdomen in the diagnostic evaluation.

Include a full blood count, white blood cell count with blood cell differential, platelet count and coagulation profile for laboratory testing. Perform directed further laboratory testing depending upon history and clinical and laboratory findings. Perform a complete evaluation of all possible causes of priapism in children.
Perform a haemoglobinopathy screen in patients with low flow priapism who are at high risk of sickle cell disease or thalassemia.
Analyse the blood gas parameters from blood aspirated from the penis to differentiate between ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism.
Perform colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum before aspiration to differentiate between ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism.
Use magnetic resonance imaging of the penis in cases of prolonged ischaemic priapism or refractory priapism, and as an adjunct to predict smooth muscle viability.

artifacts.summary: Sets out the diagnostic actions for suspected ischaemic priapism and the strength assigned to each.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports selection and sequencing of clinical examination, laboratory assessment and imaging.

artifacts.title: Table 10.4: Medical treatment of ischaemic priapism

rows:
• Intracavernous injection of 200 μg every 3-5 minutes.
• Maximum dosage is 1 mg within 1 hour.
• Lower doses are recommended in children and patients with severe cardiovascular diseases.
• Intracavernosal injection at a concentration of 2.5 mg in 1-2 mL normal saline.
• Intracavernous injection of 50-100 mg, left for 5 minutes. It is then aspirated and the penis compressed for an additional 5 minutes.
• Intracavernous injection of 2 mL of 1/100,000 adrenaline solution up to five times over a 20-minute period.
• Oral administration of 5 mg for priapism lasting more than 2.5 hours, after intracavernous injection of vasoactive agents.

artifacts.summary: Provides drug-specific doses, routes and administration instructions for medical treatment of ischaemic priapism.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Preserves dosing and population-specific cautions needed when considering the listed treatments.

artifacts.title: Figure 10.2: Management work-up of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.description: Step 1: Provide local penile anaesthesia, place a wide-bore butterfly needle of 16-18 G through the glans or laterally into the corpora cavernosa, and aspirate until bright red arterial blood appears. Step 2: Irrigate the corpora with 0.90% w/v saline solution. Step 3: Give an intracavernosal adrenoceptor agonist; the figure specifies phenylephrine in aliquots of 200 µg every 3-5 minutes until detumescence, with a maximum of 1mg within 1 hour. Reduce the phenylephrine dose in children; use caution in men with cardiovascular disease, monitor pulse and blood pressure during administration and for one hour afterwards, and do not use it in men with a history of cerebro-vascular disease or significant hypertension. Step 4: If the preceding treatment does not resolve the episode, proceed to surgical shunting; consider primary penile implantation when priapism has lasted more than 48 hours.
artifacts.summary: Presents an escalating sequence of aspiration, irrigation, intracavernosal therapy and surgery for ischaemic priapism.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Shows the treatment order and phenylephrine safety restrictions relevant to urgent management.

Step 2: It shows T-shunt ± tunnelling, penile MRI, a 'No necrosis' finding, a 'Necrosis' finding leading to PPI, and peno-scrotal decompression following a failure label. The connections between the displayed duration groups and individual procedures or findings are not fully specified in the document. Its legend defines MRI as Magnetic resonance imaging, PPI as penile prosthesis implantation and IP as ischaemic priapism.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence for treatment of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

rows: Ischaemic priapism is a medical emergency and immediate intervention is mandatory.
Erectile function preservation is directly related to the duration of ischaemic priapism, age and preoperative erectile status.
Medical treatment is variably effective in case of priapism lasting less than 48 hours
Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% results in over 80% success rate when combined with intracavernous injection of sympathomimetic drugs

Phenylephrine is the recommended drug due to its favourable safety profile in the cardiovascular system compared to other drugs. Phenylephrine is usually diluted in normal saline with a concentration of 100-500 μg/mL and given in 200 μg doses every three to five minutes directly into the corpus cavernosum. Maximum dosage is 1 mg within one hour. Patient monitoring is highly recommended.
Oral terbutaline has a success rate in up to 60% of cases when priapism is associated with intracavernous injection of erectogenic agents.
Exchange transfusion in patients with priapism associated with SCD may result in serious neurological sequelae.

Shunt procedures are effective to resolve priapism and provide pain relief. No clear recommendation of the superiority of one type of shunt over another can be given. Distal shunts are less invasive and associated with lower rate of erectile dysfunction.

Peri- and post-operative anticoagulant prophylaxis (325 mg acetylsalicylic acid pre-operatively, 5,000 IU heparin intra-operatively and 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid and 75 mg clopidogrel five days postoperatively) may prevent priapism recurrence.

Erectile dysfunction is almost inevitable in prolonged cases or ischaemic priapism. Early implantation of penile prosthesis is associated with lower infection rates and complications compared to late implantation.

artifacts.summary: Collects evidence statements and LE values for urgent treatment, medical therapy, shunting, peri-operative prophylaxis and prosthesis implantation.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Allows the reported evidence level and limitations of each treatment claim to be considered alongside management decisions.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism

rows: Start management of ischaemic priapism as early as possible (within four to six hours) and follow a stepwise approach.
Decompress the corpus cavernosum by penile aspiration and washout until fresh red blood is obtained as first treatment step.
Replace blood aspiration with intracavernous injection of a sympathomimetic drug as the first step in priapism secondary to intracavernous injections of vasoactive agents.
Perform intracavernous injection of a sympathomimetic drug in priapism that persists despite aspiration.

Repeat aspiration and intracavernous injection of a sympathomimetic drug in cases that persist despite prior aspiration and intracavernous injection of a sympathomimetic drug, before considering surgical intervention.

Treat ischaemic priapism associated with sickle cell disease in the same fashion as idiopathic ischaemic priapism. Do not use exchange transfusion as a primary treatment. Provide other supportive measures (intravenous hydration, oxygen administration with alkalisation with bicarbonate, blood exchange transfusions), but do not delay initial treatment to the penis.
Proceed to surgical treatment only when blood aspiration and intracavernous injection of sympathomimetic drugs have failed.
Perform distal shunt surgical procedures first and combine them with tunnelling if necessary.
Use proximal procedures in cases of distal shunt failure (< 48 hours) or in patients who do not wish to proceed with immediate penile implant insertion.
Discuss implantation of a penile prosthesis in cases of delayed presentation (> 48 hours) and in cases refractory to injection therapy and distal shunting.
Delay implantation of a penile prosthesis if a shunt has been performed, to minimise the risk of infection and erosion of the implant.

Decide on which type of implant to insert based on:

• patient suitability;
• surgeons’ experience; and
• availability and cost of equipment. If a malleable penile prosthesis is implanted it can be exchanged for an inflatable penile implant.

artifacts.summary: Sets out the staged treatment recommendations for ischaemic priapism, including exceptions, surgery and prosthesis decisions, with their strength ratings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Preserves the recommended order of interventions and the strength of each management recommendation.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence for treatment of stuttering priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

rows: The primary goal in the management of patients with stuttering priapism is prevention of future episodes, which can generally be achieved pharmacologically.

Hormonal therapy with GnRH agonists or antagonists or anti-androgens is able to reduce the risk of recurrent priapism episodes although it is associated with adverse events (hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido, asthenia and infertility).
Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors have a paradoxical effect in alleviating and preventing stuttering priapism, mainly in patients with idiopathic and sickle cell disease-associated priapism.
The evidence for other systemic drugs (digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin and terbutaline, hydroxyurea) is limited.

artifacts.summary: Associates evidence levels with prevention of recurrent episodes and the drug classes discussed for stuttering priapism.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Distinguishes the evidence for recurrence prevention from the more limited evidence for other systemic drugs.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism

rows: Manage each acute episode according to the treatment recommendations for ischaemic priapism (section 10.1.4).

Use hormonal therapies (mainly gonadotropin-receptor hormone agonists or antagonists) and/or anti-androgens for the prevention of future episodes in patients with frequent relapses. Do not use them before sexual maturation is reached.
Initiate treatment with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors only when the penis is in its flaccid state.
Use digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin or terbutaline only in patients with frequent and uncontrolled relapses.
Use intracavernous self-injections of sympathomimetic drugs at home for treatment of acute episodes on an interim basis until ischaemic priapism has been alleviated.

artifacts.summary: Lists recommendations for acute episodes and prevention of recurrent priapism, with eligibility restrictions and strength ratings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Separates acute treatment from preventive treatment and retains restrictions concerning sexual maturation and treatment timing.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

rows: Non-ischemic priapism is less common than ischemic and is usually associated with blunt perineal or penile trauma leading to the development of intracavernosal fistula.
Medical history and blood gas analysis are able to differentiate between ischemic and non-ischemic priapism.
Blood aspiration from the corpora in case of non-ischemic priapism reveal bright red arterial blood with normal arterial gas values.
Penile duplex US is able to identify intracavernosal fistula responsible for non-ischemic priapism.

artifacts.summary: Records evidence levels for traumatic aetiology, blood-gas findings and duplex US in non-ischaemic priapism.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports selection and interpretation of findings used to distinguish arterial from ischaemic priapism.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism

rows: Take a comprehensive history to establish the diagnosis, which can help to determine the priapism subtype.
Include a physical examination of the genitalia, perineum and abdomen in the diagnostic evaluation.
Include a neurological examination if neurogenic non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.
Include complete blood count, with white blood cell differential, and coagulation profile for laboratory testing.
Analyse the blood gas parameters from blood aspirated from the penis to differentiate between ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism.
Perform colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum to differentiate between ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism.
Perform selected pudendal arteriography when embolisation is planned for non-ischaemic priapism.

artifacts.summary: Presents the recommended diagnostic assessments for non-ischaemic priapism and their strength ratings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Clarifies when neurological examination and pudendal arteriography enter the diagnostic pathway.

artifacts.title: Summary of evidence for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.3.3.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism

rows: Non-ischaemic priapism can cause erectile dysfunction over time and early definitive management should be undertaken.

Conservative management applying ice to the perineum or site-specific perineal compression is an option in all cases. The use of androgen deprivation therapy may enable closure of the fistula reducing spontaneous and sleep-related erections.

Selective artery embolisation, using temporary or permanent substances, has high success rates. No definitive statement can be made on the best substance for embolisation in terms of sexual function preservation and success rate.
Repeated embolisation is a reasonable option for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism.
Selective surgical ligation of the fistula is associated with high risk of erectile dysfunction.

artifacts.summary: Summarises evidence for conservative treatment, embolisation and surgical ligation, including stated uncertainty about embolisation materials.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps weigh treatment options against erectile-function risks without implying that one embolisation material is established as superior.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism
artifacts.source_heading: 10.3.3.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism

rows: Perform definitive management for non-ischaemic priapism at the discretion of the treating physician as it is not a medical emergency.
Manage non-ischaemic priapism conservatively with the use of site-specific perineal compression as the first step. Consider androgen deprivation therapy only in adults.
Perform selective arterial embolisation when conservative management has failed.
Perform the first selective arterial embolisation using temporary material.
Repeat selective arterial embolisation with temporary or permanent material for recurrent non-ischaemic priapism following selective arterial embolisation.
Reserve selective surgical ligation of a fistula as a final treatment option when repeated arterial embolisation has failed.

artifacts.summary: Gives the staged recommendations for conservative management, arterial embolisation and surgical ligation, with their strength ratings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Preserves treatment order, the adult-only qualification for androgen deprivation therapy and the final-option status of surgical ligation.

document_sections.heading: There is lack of evidence to recommend one treatment over another.
document_sections.content: The evidence does not support preferring one penile enlargement treatment over another. Injectable materials considered for increasing penile girth include hyaluronic acid (HA), poly-l-lactic acid (PLA), hydroxyethyl methacrylate, polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), polyalkylamide hydrogel (PAAG), and calcium hydroxyapatite. Evidence is generally limited, although HA, PLA, and PMMA have comparatively more supporting evidence. Silicone, paraffin, and Vaseline should not be used (Strong evidence against).

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.5 Functional outcomes: sexual function, sensitivity, impact on quality of life and emotional adjustment
document_sections.content: Cosmetic interventions, including operations, may improve well-being and QoL by addressing body-related low self-esteem, anxiety, social phobia, and depressive mood. Men with genuinely short penises may seek changes in length or girth to support their sense of identity and meet cultural expectations about penile size and function. Outcomes of augmentation techniques appear mixed. A cited study of fillers reported better genital self-image and self-esteem and fewer PDD symptoms, without improvement in self-confidence or satisfaction with sexual relationships. A cited study suggested that lengthening or girth-enhancement surgery in men with normal penile size may be followed by low satisfaction and impaired erectile function and sensitivity, although increased satisfaction has also been reported. Male genital self-image has been linked to the IIEF domains of sexual desire, orgasmic and erectile function, intercourse satisfaction, and overall satisfaction. Perceived size appears more predictive of erectile function than measured size. Dissatisfaction with one's penis has been associated with less penetrative and receptive oral sex. Further research should clarify effects on patients' and partners' well-being and QoL. Compared with controls, men with BDD have shown poorer erectile and orgasmic function and less intercourse satisfaction; men with SPA have shown lower satisfaction. Sexual desire appeared unaffected in BDD and SPA.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.6 Final remarks
document_sections.content: Complaints of a short penis differ in presentation and cause: some patients have anatomical or pathological findings, whereas others do not. Surgical and non-surgical options address different causes. Detected psychopathological symptoms require referral for further medical diagnosis. Care for short-penis syndrome calls for a multidisciplinary approach that accounts for medical and ethical issues. Most reported outcomes rest on sparse evidence.

document_sections.heading: 10. PRIAPISM
document_sections.content: Priapism is an erection that persists or lasts unusually long without sexual stimulation and does not resolve. Its forms are ischaemic, non-ischaemic, and stuttering priapism. The guidance draws on three systematic reviews concerning medical and surgical care of ischaemic and non-ischaemic priapism and management of priapism associated with sickle cell disease.

document_sections.heading: 10.1 Ischaemic (Low-Flow or Veno-Occlusive) Priapism
document_sections.content: This section addresses the low-flow, veno-occlusive form of priapism.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology and Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Ischaemic priapism involves a persistent erection with rigid corpora cavernosa and minimal or absent cavernous arterial inflow. It is the commonest subtype, accounting for > 95% of all episodes. Progressive metabolic changes in the corpus cavernosum produce hypoxia, hypercapnia, glucopenia, and acidosis. Beyond 4 hours, the process resembles a compartment syndrome: ischaemia within the enclosed corpora markedly impairs cavernous circulation. Emergency treatment is needed to reduce the risk of smooth-muscle necrosis, corporal fibrosis, and permanent erectile dysfunction (ED). Duration is the strongest predictor of irreversible harm, including ED; treatment begun beyond 48-72 hours may lessen erection and pain but offers little clinical benefit for prevention of long-term ED. Most cases have no identifiable specific pathophysiological cause. Recognised contributors include sickle cell disease (SCD), haematological disorders, neoplastic syndromes, and drugs such as intracavernosal PGE1 therapy. Following injection of erectogenic agents, reported occurrence is 0.4-35%; risk is greater with papaverine-based combinations, while priapism after prostaglandin E1 injection occurs in < 1%. Among published drug-induced cases, second-generation antipsychotics accounted for 33.8%, other medications for 11.3%, and alpha-adrenergic antagonists for 8.8%. Priapism has only occasionally been reported in PDE5Is users. FDA Adverse Reporting System Public Dashboard data attributed 2.9% of drug-induced cases to PDE5Is, but most affected men had other risk factors, so whether PDE5Is themselves cause ischaemic priapism remains unclear; their use alone is generally not considered a risk factor. SCD accounts for 63% of childhood cases and is the primary cause in 23% of adult cases. Several penile signalling pathways may contribute to SCD-associated priapism. Contrary to earlier assumptions, maintaining physiological testosterone does not cause priapism and instead supports penile homeostasis and ordinary erectile function. Testosterone deficiency remains a disputed risk factor: it is common in SCD, but recent evidence suggests it might not increase priapism risk. Malignant priapism due to regional or metastatic infiltration is uncommon and most often originates from bladder or prostate cancer. In a retrospective study of 412 men with ischaemic priapism, eleven (3.5%) had malignant priapism; seven cases resulted from local invasion, and the remainder from haematological malignancy. Conventional pharmacological measures are unlikely to work in these patients. All should undergo penile MRI and receive supportive care and treatment for their primary cancer; palliative penectomy may be considered in selected patients whose penile pain persists despite palliative options. Partial priapism, also called idiopathic partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavemosum, is rare. Often classified as priapism confined to a single crura, it involves a corpus cavernosum thrombus rather than ischaemia. Its cause is unknown; reported associations include cycling, trauma, drug use, intercourse, haematological disease, and α-blocker use. A congenital corporal web is another risk factor. Table 10.1 catalogues idiopathic, haematological, vascular, infectious, metabolic, neurogenic, neoplastic, and medication-related aetiological factors.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.1.1 Summary of evidence on the epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology of ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: The evidence table assigns LE 1b to the findings that ischaemic priapism comprises more than 95% of cases, that most cases are idiopathic, and that sickle cell disease is the leading childhood cause. It assigns LE 2a to the comparison of about 5% occurrence after intracavernous papaverinebased combinations with < 1% after prostaglandin E1 alone. Sporadic reports of priapism among PDE5Is users carry LE 4.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Evaluation distinguishes priapism subtypes and investigates potential causes.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2.1 History
document_sections.content: A detailed history is central to diagnosis and treatment. Ask specifically about SCD and other haematological abnormalities, pelvic, genital, or perineal injury, erection duration, pain and its severity, prescribed and recreational drugs, earlier priapism and its treatment, and erectile function before the latest episode. These details help identify the subtype, as illustrated in Table 10.2. Ischaemic episodes typically involve increasing penile pain and a rigid erection; non-ischaemic episodes are often painless, with variable rigidity.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2.2 Physical examination
document_sections.content: In ischaemic priapism, the corpora are completely rigid and tender while the glans remains soft; severe pain is usual. Pelvic examination can disclose a pelvic or genitourinary malignancy.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2.3 Laboratory testing
document_sections.content: Initial tests should comprise a complete blood count, white blood cell count and differential, platelet count, and coagulation profile to evaluate anaemia and haematological abnormalities. Corporal blood aspiration is a mandatory initial investigation and usually yields dark, ischaemic blood. Blood gas testing is essential to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism; Table 10.3 presents characteristic values. Further tests should follow the history, examination, and initial results and may include haemoglobin electrophoresis to diagnose SCD or another haemoglobinopathy.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2.4 Penile imaging
document_sections.content: After clinical diagnosis, colour Doppler US of the penis and perineum is recommended as an alternative or addition to blood gas analysis for distinguishing the subtypes. It can detect a fistula-related blush with 100% sensitivity and 73% specificity. In ischaemic priapism, perform penile ultrasound before corporal aspiration: intervention can create atypical flow resembling non-ischaemic priapism or reperfusion. Penile MRI may assist selected ischaemic cases by evaluating corporal viability and fibrosis, particularly in refractory episodes or presentation after > 48 hours. In a prospective study of 38 patients, MRI predicted biopsy-correlated non-viable smooth muscle with 100% sensitivity. Every patient whose MRI indicated viable muscle retained erectile function during clinical follow-up; those with non-viable muscle were offered early prosthesis placement.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: The evidence summary assigns LE 3 to the diagnostic value of medical history, corporal blood gas analysis, blood count and haemoglobinopathy screening, pre-aspiration penile Colour Doppler US, and penile MRI for predicting non-viable smooth muscle. Obtain a comprehensive history to establish the diagnosis and help identify the subtype (Strong). Examine the genitalia, perineum, and abdomen (Strong). Obtain a full blood count, white blood cell count with differential, platelet count, and coagulation profile; tailor additional tests to the history and clinical and laboratory findings, and investigate every possible cause in children (Strong). Screen for haemoglobinopathies in patients with low-flow priapism who are at high risk for sickle cell disease or thalassemia (Strong). Analyse gases in aspirated penile blood to differentiate ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism (Strong). Perform colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum before aspiration for this distinction (Strong). Use penile magnetic resonance imaging in prolonged or refractory ischaemic priapism as an additional means of predicting smooth-muscle viability (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Acute ischaemic priapism is a medical emergency requiring urgent, sequential intervention. Treatment seeks painless detumescence and prevention of corporal smooth-muscle fibrosis and subsequent ED.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1 Medical Management – first-line treatment
document_sections.content: Medical first-line therapy is strongly recommended before surgery for ischaemic episodes lasting more than 4 hours. When initiated beyond 48 hours, such measures may relieve the erection but have little documented value for preserving long-term erectile function, probably because irreversible hypoxic muscle injury begins by approximately 48 hours. In a series of 50 successfully treated patients followed for a mean of 66 months, priapism lasting more than 48 hours was associated with a significant ED risk. Previously described measures include exercise, ejaculation, ice packs, cold baths, and cold-water enemas. Evidence of benefit is limited, and these measures may worsen the condition in SCD; outcomes for conservative measures alone are seldom reported. One small series reported detumescence in six out of ten cases after cold-water enemas. Another study found that cooling the penis and perineum and walking upstairs produced detumescence in 24.5% of 122 patients whose episodes lasted more than 6 hours.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1.1 Penile anaesthesia/analgesia
document_sections.content: Aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetic injection can be performed without anaesthesia, but severe penile pain may warrant it. Local cutaneous anaesthesia can make subsequent treatment easier even when it does not relieve ischaemic pain. Options are dorsal nerve block, circumferential penile block, subcutaneous penile-shaft block, and oral conscious sedation for paediatric patients.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1.2 Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution
document_sections.content: For an episode lasting more than 4 hours, initial intervention is aspiration of stagnant corporal blood to relieve the compartment-like state. The corpus cavernosum can be entered through the glans or laterally through the proximal shaft with a 16 or 18 G angio-catheter or butterfly needle, traversing skin, subcutaneous tissue, and tunica albuginea. Some clinicians use two needles or catheters to hasten drainage or aspirate while simultaneously irrigating with saline. Continue aspiration until the returned blood is bright red and oxygenated. Most published first-line series combined aspiration and irrigation with intracavernosal sympathomimetics, preventing a reliable estimate of aspiration plus irrigation alone; reported success across case series and retrospective studies ranges from 0 to 100%. An RCT involving 70 patients whose injection-associated ischaemic priapism lasted more than 6 hours reported 85% success with aspiration and temperature-varied saline irrigation; a 10°C infusion after aspiration gave the best results. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether adding saline irrigation improves on aspiration alone.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1.3 Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents.
document_sections.content: Combining aspiration, with or without irrigation, and intracavernous medication is considered standard care for ischaemic priapism. Sympathomimetic or α-adrenergic agents used include phenylephrine, etilephrine, ephedrine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and metaraminol; reported resolution reaches up to 80%. Intracavernous adrenaline alone has also been described sporadically. Reported resolution with prior aspiration or irrigation plus a sympathomimetic ranges from 80 to 100%, versus 58% with sympathomimetic injection alone. Phenylephrine and other intracavernous sympathomimetics may cause headache, dizziness, hypertension, reflex bradycardia, tachycardia, palpitations, and, sporadically, subarachnoid haemorrhage. Monitor blood pressure and pulse during administration. Because hypertension and serious cardiovascular or neurological complications have been reported, the Guidelines Panel considers these drugs contraindicated in malignant or poorly controlled hypertension. Data also suggest a hypertensive crisis when sympathomimetics are combined with monoamine oxidase inhibitors; do not combine them.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1.4 Intracavernosal and oral pharmacological agents
document_sections.content: Table 10.4 summarises the doses and administration of medicines used for ischaemic priapism.

document_sections.heading: Phenylephrine
document_sections.content: Phenylephrine selectively activates α-1-adrenergic receptors. Small case series have observed intracavernous detumescence with few adverse effects. It is the preferred adrenergic agonist because of its α-1 selectivity without accompanying β-mediated cardiac inotropic or chronotropic effects. Cardiovascular adverse effects remain possible. Monitor pulse and blood pressure every fifteen minutes for 1 hour after injection, especially in older men with existing cardiovascular disease. After injection, compress the puncture site and massage the corpus cavernosum to distribute the medicine.

document_sections.heading: Etilephrine
document_sections.content: Etilephrine is an adrenergic agonist described as directly stimulating both  and  adrenergic receptors. Most published experience concerns SCD-associated priapism; small retrospective series also report benefit in iatrogenic cases. It is the second most frequently used sympathomimetic agent.

document_sections.heading: Methylene blue
document_sections.content: Methylene blue inhibits guanylate cyclase and may inhibit endothelial-mediated relaxation of cavernous smooth muscle. Small retrospective case series report successful treatment of short-duration pharmacologically induced priapism. Reported adverse effects are temporary burning and blue penile discolouration.

document_sections.heading: Adrenaline
document_sections.content: Adrenaline is described as having both -adrenergic receptor agonist and -adrenergic receptor activity. Intracavernous use has been reported for ischaemic priapism following injection of vasoactive drugs. Limited reports suggest it can resolve short-duration episodes; one small series reported success in over 50% after one injection and 95% overall after repeated injections.

document_sections.heading: β-2-agonists
document_sections.content: Oral terbutaline is a β-2-agonist with minor β-1 and some α-agonist activity; its mechanism in this setting is not fully understood. Its principal use is prevention of recurrent prolonged erections. Three placebo-controlled RCTs of injection-associated ischemic priapism reported success in 30 to 60%. Use caution with coronary artery disease, increased intravascular fluid volume, oedema, or hypokalaemia. One multi-centre prospective study reported detumescence in 34% with salbutamol after an injection-associated prolonged erection lasting more than 3 hours. Stronger evidence is required before oral salbutamol can be recommended for ischaemic priapism.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.1.5 Management of priapism related to sickle cell disease
document_sections.content: A systematic review found few studies confined to SCD patients; studies of mixed populations generally did not present SCD-specific results. Inconsistent reporting of patient characteristics, treatments, and outcomes, variable reported follow-up, and generally poor study quality prevented high-quality evidence-based recommendations. Urgent penile intervention follows the general ischaemic-priapism approach and should be coordinated with a haematologist. Additional SCD-directed measures may be needed. Provide intravenous hydration and narcotic analgesia while preparing aspiration and irrigation; supplemental oxygen and bicarbonate alkalinisation may also help. Measure haemoglobin S (HbS) percentage in every SCD patient with acute priapism. Exchange transfusion has been proposed to improve oxygen delivery; donor blood should be sickle cell haemoglobin negative and matched for Rh and Kell antigens. Whether exchange transfusion itself resolves priapism is uncertain. A systematic review reported mean time to detumescence of eleven days with exchange transfusion versus eight days with conventional care, and 9 cases of transfusion-associated ASPEN syndrome. A series of 10 SCD patients reported safe exchange transfusion, but other reports suggest serious neurological sequelae. Do not use exchange transfusion routinely as the primary intervention unless SCD-related symptoms pose a risk. After failed medical care, transfusion may be needed to allow safe general anaesthesia before definitive surgery.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.2 Surgical management- second-line treatments
document_sections.content: Second-line care generally consists of shunting or penile prosthesis placement for refractory or delayed ischaemic priapism and should follow failure of medical options. Evidence does not establish when to move to surgery, although at least 1 hour of unsuccessful first-line treatment may be considered. Persistent corporal rigidity, cavernosal acidosis, anoxia, marked glucopenia, absent cavernosal arterial inflow on colour duplex US, and raised intracorporal pressure suggest first-line failure.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.2.1 Penile shunt surgery
document_sections.content: A penile shunt drains ischaemic blood from a corpus cavernosum toward spongiosal tissue, the glans, or a vein through an opening in the tunica albuginea, allowing circulation to recover. Procedure selection reflects surgeon preference and experience; distal shunts conventionally precede proximal ones. Assess success through penile rigidity or repeat testing such as cavernous blood gases. Colour US may mislead during post-decompression hyperaemic reperfusion. Recovery of erectile function after shunting for prolonged priapism is low and depends directly on episode duration, pre-operative erectile function, and age. If ischaemia resolves within 24 hours, reported recovery of spontaneous functional erections, with or without PDE5Is, is 78-100%. Other studies associate durations beyond 36-48 hours with corporal structural and functional injury and ED > 90%. Shunting after 36-48 hours may relieve only pain rather than preserve erectile function; early prosthesis placement can be considered. Tunical incision exposes collagen to blood coagulation factors and activates clotting, providing a rationale for peri-operative anti-coagulation. Following unsuccessful aspiration, one study reported an 84% reduction in recurrence with peri-procedural anti-thrombotic treatment—325 mg acetylsalicylic acid pre-operatively, 5000 IU intraoperative heparin, then 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid and 75 mg clopidogrel post-operatively for 5 days—versus no such treatment. Four categories of shunts have been reported. Limited evidence cannot establish overall superiority, but distal shunts are less invasive, have lower post-operative ED rates, and are recommended as the first surgical choice.

document_sections.heading: Percutaneous distal (corpora-glanular) shunts
document_sections.content: Winter’s procedure creates a channel between the glans and each corpus cavernosum using a Trucut biopsy needle. Post-operative sequelae are uncommon. Although straightforward, it has been reported as the least successful distal shunt: its 1.6 mm (14-18 g) needle opening may inadequately drain post-ischaemic hyperaemia, increasing intracavernous pressure and promoting early closure. Ebbehoj’s technique repeatedly passes a size 11 blade percutaneously to create multiple tunical windows between the glans and both distal corporal tips. A T-Shunt uses a size 10 blade passed through the glans lateral to the urethral meatus into a corporal tip, turned 90° laterally, and withdrawn; the other side is treated if needed. T-shunt tunnelling may then use a size 8/10 Hegar dilator, potentially under US guidance to reduce urethral injury. Glanular entry sites are sutured after detumescence. Tunnelling with a 7 mm metal sound or 7/8 Hegar dilator is necessary when priapism lasts > 48 hours. This approach may combine distal-shunt access with proximal corporal drainage and potentially reduce the profibrotic effect of retained blood.

document_sections.heading: Open distal (corpora-glanular) shunts
document_sections.content: Al-Ghorab’s procedure removes circular cone-shaped segments of distal tunica albuginea bilaterally through the glans, then closes the glans with a running absorbable suture. A transverse glanular incision may impair arterial inflow because distal deep dorsal arteries run lengthwise. Burnett’s technique (Snake manoeuvre) modifies this shunt by passing a 7/8 Hegar dilator retrogradely into each distal corpus through the Al-Ghorab opening, removing it, and compressing the penis from proximal to distal to evacuate blood before glanular closure. Reported complications are wound infection, penile skin necrosis, and urethrocutaneous fistulae.

document_sections.heading: Open proximal (corpora-spongiosal) shunts
document_sections.content: Quackles’s technique creates an open connection between a proximal corpus cavernosum and the corpus spongiosum through a trans-scrotal or perineal approach. Common complications include unintended urethro-cavernous fistula, urethral stricture, and cavernositis. A perineal approach to the spongiosal bulb reduces urethral-injury risk. Proximal shunts are more invasive and have higher documented ED rates.

document_sections.heading: Peno-scrotal decompression
document_sections.content: A newer glans-sparing proximal decompression technique opens the proximal corpus cavernosum and tunnels proximally and distally with a suction tip; high success has been described. In a cohort of 25 patients, 12 had undergone previous corpora-glanular shunting. Recurrence followed unilateral peno-scrotal decompression in two of 25; among the 15 with follow-up, 40% had ED. Although promising, PSD for refractory priapism may delay prosthesis placement and thereby worsen outcomes, including penile shortening and prosthetic infection.

document_sections.heading: Vein anastomoses/shunts
document_sections.content: Grayhack’s procedure mobilises the saphenous vein beneath its femoral-vein junction and connects it end-to-side to a corpus cavernosum. Possible venous-shunt complications include saphenofemoral thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.2.2 Immediate penile prosthesis implantation
document_sections.content: Evidence on implantation principally comprises retrospective, non-randomised case series with variable follow-up; studies report priapism resolution, sexual function, and surgical adverse events. Refractory acute ischaemic priapism or episodes lasting more than 48 hours generally cause complete ED and may cause substantial long-term deformity; immediate prosthesis implantation is advocated in these circumstances. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI and cavernosal smooth-muscle biopsy can identify necrosis, which suggests that shunting will probably fail, and can inform counselling and decisions after refractory disease or presentation at > 48 hours. Compared with late insertion, early implantation is associated with lower infection rates (6-7% vs. 19-30%), penile shortening (3% vs. 40%), and revision rates (9% vs. 27%). Reported overall satisfaction is 96% with early versus 60% with late implantation. Distal erosion, infection, and revision remain possible. Early placement may preserve penile length and girth and avert fibrosis-related curvature; later exchange to an inflatable device may permit larger cylinders. Choose the implant according to patient suitability, surgeon experience, and equipment availability and cost. Immediate malleable prosthesis insertion is recommended to avoid difficulties and complications of delayed surgery in fibrotic corpora. No randomised trials compare malleable with inflatable prostheses. Immediate inflatable placement may be undertaken in suitably counselled, motivated patients, but a semi-rigid device is generally more suitable because implantation is easier and shorter, potentially reducing infection risk. An immediately placed inflatable device must be cycled at once to prevent a contracting fibrous capsule; early cycling helps prevent curvature and shortening. There are no clear indications mandating immediate implantation in acute cases, though it can be considered for delayed or refractory disease. Relative indications are ischaemia lasting more than 48 hours; unsuccessful aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetics in delayed priapism (> 48 hours); MRI or biopsy evidence of muscle necrosis; unsuccessful shunting, although delayed cases (> 48 hours) may proceed to implantation before a shunt; and refractory disease after shunting. The optimal placement window is within the first three weeks after the episode. After shunting, implantation can be delayed to permit oedema reduction and wound healing and lower infection risk; a vacuum device may be used meanwhile to limit fibrosis and shortening.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.3.2.3 Surgery for non-acute sequelae after ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: Later consequences include corporal necrosis and fibrosis, scarring, megalophallic deformity, shortening, occasional penile loss, and frequent ED. These can occur even after apparently successful first- or second-line detumescence. A penile prosthesis is sometimes indicated for severe ED in SCD because PDE5Is and intracavernous injections are avoided owing to possible recurrent priapism. Narrow-based implants are preferable with extensive fibrosis because insertion needs less dilatation. Severe tissue destruction or complex deformity may require altered surgical techniques. When concomitant prosthesis placement is considered, options include multiple corporotomies, corporal excavation, optical corporotomy-Shaeer technique, dilatation with Carrion-Rosello cavernotome, Uramix or Mooreville cavernotome, removal of scar tissue, a small-diameter prosthesis, or graft-based penile reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 10.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: The evidence summary identifies ischaemic priapism as an emergency requiring immediate intervention (LE 2b). Preservation of erectile function depends on episode duration, age, and preoperative erectile status (LE 2b). Medical treatment before 48 hours has variable effectiveness (LE 2b). Aspiration with or without irrigation using 0.9% saline achieves over 80% success when paired with intracavernous sympathomimetics (LE 2b). Phenylephrine is favoured for its comparative cardiovascular safety; the summary describes dilution to 100-500 μg/mL and administration of 200 μg every three to five minutes, up to 1 mg within one hour, with patient monitoring strongly advised (LE 2b). Oral terbutaline achieves success in up to 60% of injection-associated cases (LE 1b). Exchange transfusion in SCD-associated priapism may produce serious neurological sequelae (LE 2b). Shunts resolve priapism and pain; no type has proven superiority, although distal shunts are less invasive and associated with less ED (LE 2b). Peri- and post-operative prophylaxis comprising 325 mg acetylsalicylic acid pre-operatively, 5,000 IU heparin intra-operatively, and 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid plus 75 mg clopidogrel five days postoperatively may reduce recurrence (LE 3). ED is nearly unavoidable in prolonged cases, while early prosthesis placement has fewer infections and complications than late placement (LE 2b). Begin stepwise management as soon as possible, within four to six hours (Strong). Start by aspirating and washing out the corpora until fresh red blood appears (Strong). For priapism caused by intracavernous vasoactive injections, use intracavernous sympathomimetic injection instead of aspiration as the initial step (Strong). Inject a sympathomimetic if aspiration does not resolve priapism (Strong), and repeat aspiration and sympathomimetic injection after failure of both before considering surgery (Strong). Treat SCD-associated ischaemic priapism as idiopathic ischaemic priapism; do not make exchange transfusion the primary treatment. Supply supportive intravenous hydration, oxygen with bicarbonate alkalisation, and blood exchange transfusions when appropriate without postponing initial penile treatment (Strong). Operate only after aspiration and intracavernous sympathomimetics fail (Strong). Use distal shunts first, adding tunnelling when necessary (Weak). Use proximal procedures after distal-shunt failure at < 48 hours or when the patient declines immediate implantation (Weak). Discuss prosthesis implantation for presentation at > 48 hours or disease refractory to injections and distal shunting (Weak). If shunting was performed, postpone prosthesis placement to reduce infection and erosion (Strong). Base implant selection on suitability, surgeon experience, and equipment availability and cost; a malleable implant can subsequently be exchanged for an inflatable one (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 10.2 Priapism in Special Situations
document_sections.content: This section covers recurrent priapism and priapism in children.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1 Stuttering (recurrent or intermittent) priapism
document_sections.content: Stuttering, intermittent, or recurrent priapism consists of repeated painful prolonged erections that resolve spontaneously between episodes. Episodes resemble recurrent ischaemic priapism but are generally shorter; their frequency and duration vary, and one can develop into prolonged ischaemic priapism. Robust epidemiological evidence is lacking. Recurrent episodes occur in 42-64% of men with SCD. Among adolescents and young men, reported priapism incidence is 35%, of whom 72% have a stuttering-priapism history. Causes resemble those of ischaemic priapism: SCD is most common, but idiopathic and neurologically associated cases occur. Acute ischaemic priapism, particularly lasting more than 4 hours, increases subsequent risk. Proposed mechanisms include inflammation, cellular adhesion, NO metabolism, vascular reactivity, and coagulation. An androgen association is disputed; lowering serum testosterone to hypogonadal levels is one proposed means of suppressing androgen-related triggers of recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.1 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: History, examination, laboratory investigation, and imaging follow the principles used for ischaemic priapism. Ask about recurring prolonged erections, which may arise several times daily or only once every few months, continuously or with episode-free intervals lasting months or years. Episodes usually begin during sleep and do not resolve on waking. They are painful and rigid, as in ischaemic priapism, but typically shorter and may prompt first presentation. Between episodes the penis is usually normal, although fibrosis can occur; rarely it becomes enlarged, termed megalo-phallus. Diagnostic recommendations are the same as those in section 10.1.2.5.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2 Disease management
document_sections.content: Management chiefly aims to prevent recurrence and reduce progression to prolonged ischaemic priapism resistant to usual treatment. Pharmacological prevention is sufficient in most cases. Treat each acute episode similarly to ischaemic priapism, using aspiration and irrigation together with intracavernous α-adrenergic agonists.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.1 α-Adrenergic agonists
document_sections.content: Studies suggest possible preventive benefit from daily oral α-adrenergic agonists; tachycardia and palpitations are potential adverse effects. Pseudoephedrine may be a first-line option, although its action on corporal smooth muscle is not fully established. Oral etilephrine has been used to prevent SCD-associated recurrence at 5-10 mg daily, with responses up to 72%. One placebo-controlled RCT comparing etilephrine with ephedrine prophylaxis found no efficacy difference between the medicines.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.2 Hormonal manipulations of circulating testosterone
document_sections.content: Hormonal treatment lowers circulating testosterone to suppress androgen effects on erection. Approaches include GnRH agonists or antagonists, antiandrogens, and oestrogens. Possible adverse effects are hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, reduced libido, and asthenia. The approaches appear similarly effective, but potential cardiovascular toxicity restricts oestrogen use. Other endocrine options used with some success are 5-α-reductase inhibitors and ketoconazole, which reduces adrenal and testicular androgen production. Evidence does not permit conclusions about dose, duration, or efficacy needed for sustained suppression. Exercise strong caution in pre-pubertal boys and adolescents and seek paediatric endocrinology advice. Hormonal agents have contraceptive effects, disrupt sexual maturation and spermatogenesis, and affect fertility. Counsel men seeking conception with their partners thoroughly; sperm cryopreservation may be considered to reduce possible fertility consequences of anti-androgen therapy.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.3 Digoxin
document_sections.content: Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside and positive inotrope used for congestive heart failure; its effects on smooth-muscle tone through several pathways can promote detumescence. Reported maintenance treatment with 0.25-0.5 mg/daily in idiopathic stuttering priapism reduces hospital visits and improves QoL. In a small double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study, digoxin lowered sexual desire, excitement, and penile rigidity without a significant change in circulating testosterone, oestrogens, or LH. Possible adverse effects include reduced libido, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion, blurred vision, headache, gynaecomastia, rash, and arrhythmia.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.4 Terbutaline
document_sections.content: Terbutaline has been used to prevent recurrence; reported detumescence in alprostadil-induced priapism is 36%. The only RCT, involving n = 68 patients with pharmacologically induced priapism, found detumescence in 42% of the terbutaline group versus 15% of the placebo group. Adverse effects include nervousness, shakiness, drowsiness, palpitations, headache, dizziness, hot flushes, nausea, and weakness.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.5 Gabapentin
document_sections.content: Gabapentin has anticonvulsant, antinociceptive, and anxiolytic properties. Its proposed action is inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels and reduced synaptic transmission; reductions in testosterone and FSH have also been described. A reported regimen is 400 mg, four times daily, up to 2,400 mg daily until complete detumescence, followed by maintenance at 300 mg/daily. Reported adverse effects are anorgasmia and impaired erectile function.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.6 Baclofen
document_sections.content: Baclofen, a gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) derivative and muscle relaxant, can inhibit erection and ejaculation through GABA activity and prevent recurrent reflexogenic or neurologically related prolonged erections. Oral treatment has little efficacy and is not usually used for stuttering priapism; intrathecal treatment is more effective. Possible adverse effects are drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, headache, hypotension, and nausea.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.7 Hydroxyurea
document_sections.content: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, blocking deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis and arresting cells in S-phase. It is an established treatment for improving SCD and life expectancy. Evidence for preventing recurrent priapism is limited. Reported adverse effects include oligozoospermia and leg ulcers.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.8 Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: Low-dose PDE5Is can paradoxically lessen and prevent recurrence, principally in idiopathic and SCD-associated stuttering priapism. Begin treatment only while the penis is flaccid, not during an acute episode. Benefit takes one week to appear. Impaired male sexual function has not been reported.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.9 Intracavernosal injections
document_sections.content: Because systemic prevention may not work immediately, some patients may temporarily need home intracavernous self-injection of sympathomimetics; phenylephrine and etilephrine are most commonly used. Tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) converts plasminogen to the fibrinolytic enzyme plasmin. Limited clinical evidence suggests that one intracavernous TPA injection may treat recalcitrant priapism. Mild bleeding is the most frequently observed adverse effect.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.2.10 Penile prosthesis
document_sections.content: Patients with medically refractory stuttering priapism often require emergency visits and remain at risk of a major ischaemic episode; prosthesis placement can reduce that risk. Do not offer a prosthesis for prevention before medical treatment, and reserve it as a last resort for carefully selected patients. For permanent ED caused by stuttering priapism, use ED medicines cautiously because they may provoke an ischaemic episode; prosthesis placement can be considered.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of stuttering priapism
document_sections.content: Prevention of future episodes is the primary aim and is usually possible with medicines (LE 2b). GnRH agonists or antagonists and anti-androgens can reduce recurrence but may cause hot flushes, gynaecomastia, ED, loss of libido, asthenia, and infertility (LE 3). Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors can paradoxically reduce and prevent episodes, especially in idiopathic and SCD-associated disease (LE 3). Evidence for digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin, terbutaline, and hydroxyurea is limited (LE 3). Treat each acute episode according to the ischaemic-priapism recommendations in section 10.1.4 (Strong). For frequent relapse, use hormonal treatment, mainly gonadotropin-receptor hormone agonists or antagonists, and/or anti-androgens to prevent episodes, but not before sexual maturation (Weak). Start phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors only in the flaccid state (Weak). Restrict digoxin, α-adrenergic agonists, baclofen, gabapentin, and terbutaline to frequent, uncontrolled relapse (Weak). Home intracavernous sympathomimetic self-injections may temporarily treat acute episodes until ischaemic priapism has been alleviated (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 10.2.1.4 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Use history and examination to assess whether treatment prevents or reduces recurrent erections and to evaluate erectile function and penile fibrosis.

document_sections.heading: 10.2.2 Priapism in children
document_sections.content: Children have the same ischaemic, stuttering, and non-ischaemic categories as adults, plus a described neonatal form. Paediatric priapism is considered rare, but prevalence data are unavailable. SCD is the leading cause, followed by leukaemia (10%), trauma (10%), idiopathic causes (19%), and drugs (5%). One study reported pre-pubertal SCD-related priapism in 25% of children. Another found that 90% of men with SCD experienced their first episode before age 20 years. Prompt investigation and treatment are important because untreated ischaemic disease can lead to adult ED and psychosexual problems. Care should be multidisciplinary, with haematology and paediatric endocrinology input.

document_sections.heading: 10.3 Non-ischaemic (high-flow or arterial) priapism
document_sections.content: Non-ischaemic priapism is a persistent erection caused by uncontrolled arterial inflow to the cavernous tissue. Its aetiological categories are traumatic, neurogenic, iatrogenic, and idiopathic.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.1 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Epidemiological estimates largely come from small case series. Non-ischaemic priapism is significantly less common than ischaemic priapism and represents only 5% of cases. Blunt perineal or penile injury is the commonest cause. Laceration of a cavernous artery or branch creates an artery-to-lacunar-space fistula, increasing flow and causing a prolonged erection. Onset after trauma may be delayed up to two to three weeks, possibly because arterial spasm or ischaemic necrosis precedes fistula formation. Priapism typically emerges after nocturnal or sexually related erection raises cavernous arterial flow and pressure. Erections are usually incompletely rigid and painless because venous drainage persists and tissue does not become ischaemic. Acute spinal cord injury may also cause this form, presumably through loss of sympathetic input and predominance of parasympathetic-driven arterial flow. Other reported antecedents are internal urethrotomy, Nesbit procedure, circumcision, transrectal prostate biopsy, prostate-cancer brachytherapy, and shunting for ischaemic priapism that lacerates a cavernous artery and converts low to high flow. Occasional high-flow cases occur with SCD, but their mechanism is unclear. Penile metastatic malignancy is another rare cause.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Diagnostic assessment combines history, examination, laboratory investigation, and penile imaging to distinguish arterial from ischaemic priapism.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2.1 History
document_sections.content: A comprehensive history is mandatory and follows the principles for ischaemic priapism. Suspect arterial disease after pelvic, perineal, or genital injury when erection persists without full rigidity or penile pain, although discomfort is possible. Sexual stimulation can produce full rigidity, so intercourse is usually preserved. Post-traumatic onset may follow the injury by several hours to weeks.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2.2 Physical examination
document_sections.content: The corpora are swollen but not completely rigid. Abdominal, penile, and perineal examination can reveal injury. Add neurological examination when a neurogenic cause is suspected.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2.3 Laboratory testing
document_sections.content: Obtain a blood count with white-cell differential and coagulation profile to investigate anaemia or other haematological abnormalities. Corporal aspiration yields bright red arterial blood in arterial priapism, unlike the dark blood of ischaemic priapism. Blood gas testing is essential for differentiation; high-flow results resemble normal arterial blood, as shown in Table 10.3.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2.4 Penile imaging
document_sections.content: Colour duplex US of the penis and perineum is recommended to distinguish the subtypes and must be performed without intracavernosal vasoactive injection. It can localise the fistula by a colour blush and turbulent, high-velocity Doppler flow; cavernous arterial velocities are normal to high. Selective pudendal arteriography can show a characteristic blush at the injury site, but its invasiveness warrants reserving it for cases in which embolisation is contemplated. MRI has a controversial diagnostic role and limited value here because small penile vessels and fistulae are difficult to show.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of non-ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: The evidence summary associates the less common non-ischaemic form with blunt penile or perineal trauma and an intracavernosal fistula (LE 2b). History and blood gases distinguish it from ischaemic disease (LE 2b). Aspirated blood is bright red with normal arterial gas values (LE 2b), and penile duplex US can identify the causative fistula (LE 2b). Obtain a comprehensive history to establish diagnosis and subtype (Strong). Examine genitalia, perineum, and abdomen (Strong); add neurological examination if a neurogenic cause is suspected (Strong). Obtain a complete blood count with white-cell differential and a coagulation profile (Strong). Analyse gases from aspirated penile blood (Strong), and perform penile and perineal colour duplex ultrasound to differentiate the subtypes (Strong). Perform selective pudendal arteriography when embolisation is planned (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Traditionally, non-ischaemic priapism has not been considered an emergency because corporal blood is not ischaemic. Recent evidence nevertheless suggests duration can affect erectile function. In a series of six patients with highflow priapism, all reported ED or distal penile flaccidity after median follow-up of 4.5 (2-12) weeks. Treatment seeks to close the fistula. Initial options include observation-based conservative care or direct perineal compression; failure calls for selective arterial embolisation. The ideal interval before embolisation remains disputed. Timing of definitive management rests with the treating physician and should be discussed with the patient, including treatment risks.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Conservative options include perineal ice or usually US-guided perineal compression. A fistula sometimes closes without intervention, and intercourse can remain possible even if it stays open. Case series report that androgen deprivation using leuprolide injections, bicalutamide, or ketoconazole may promote closure by reducing spontaneous and sleep-related erections; resulting sexual dysfunction must be considered. ED or distal penile flaccidity may arise during conservative care. Aspiration does not help treat arterial priapism. α-adrenergic antagonists are not recommended because of possible serious adverse effects, including passage into the systemic circulation.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.2 Selective arterial embolisation
document_sections.content: Temporary embolic materials include autologous blood clot and gel foam; permanent options include microcoils, ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer (PVA), and N-butyl-cyanoacrylate (NBCA). It has been hypothesised that temporary materials lower ED risk but increase failure or recurrence; evidence is insufficient to support that assumption. Reported success after a first embolization ranges between 61.7 and 83.3%, and ED rates from 0-33.3%. These findings suggest that recurrence may not be significantly higher with temporary materials and preservation of erectile function may not differ much between temporary and permanent approaches. Other possible complications are penile gangrene, gluteal ischaemia, cavernositis, and perineal abscess. Repeat embolisation is a reasonable option in terms of both efficacy and safety.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.3 Surgical management
document_sections.content: Fistula ligation can be undertaken through a transcorporeal or inguinoscrotal approach with intraoperative Doppler US. The operation is technically difficult and carries substantial risks, particularly ED. It is rarely performed and should be considered only if selective embolisation is contraindicated or unavailable or repeated procedures have failed. It may be appropriate for someone seeking definitive treatment who is sexually inactive or already has ED. Reported ED after treatment for nonischaemic priapism ranges from 0-50%, with the highest rates following surgical ligation. Long-term ED may require a penile prosthesis.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of non-ischaemic priapism
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that non-ischaemic priapism can eventually cause ED and supports early definitive management (LE 3). Perineal ice or targeted compression is an option in every case, while androgen deprivation may aid fistula closure by reducing spontaneous and sleep-related erections (LE 3). Selective embolisation with temporary or permanent materials has high success rates, but evidence cannot establish the best material for success or preservation of sexual function (LE 3). Repeat embolisation is a reasonable option (LE 2b). Selective surgical ligation has a high ED risk (LE 3). Leave the timing of definitive treatment to the treating physician because this condition is not a medical emergency (Weak). First use conservative targeted perineal compression, considering androgen deprivation only in adults (Weak). Perform selective arterial embolisation after conservative failure (Strong), using temporary material for the first procedure (Weak). For recurrence after embolisation, repeat the procedure with temporary or permanent material (Weak). Reserve selective fistula ligation as the final option after repeated embolisation has failed (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.5 High-flow priapism in children
document_sections.content: Non-ischaemic priapism is particularly rare in children. Reluctance to discuss symptoms with parents may contribute to missed diagnosis and underestimated prevalence. Causes, presentation, investigation, and treatment principles are broadly similar to adults, with some differences. Idiopathic disease occurs in a significant proportion of children. Thumb compression of the perineum may help distinguish subtypes, especially in children: immediate detumescence followed by renewed erection when pressure is removed can occur. Perineal ice or targeted compression may work particularly well in children. Embolisation has been reported as successful but is technically challenging and should be performed in a specialist paediatric vascular radiology department.

document_sections.heading: 10.3.3.6 Follow-up
document_sections.content: During conservative care, examination and colour duplex US may help judge effectiveness. Close surveillance with colour duplex US and MRI can identify distal penile fibrosis and inform earlier embolisation. After selective embolisation, follow-up should include clinical examination, colour duplex US, and assessment of erectile function; repeat arteriography if findings are uncertain. Follow-up evaluates treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical or functional consequences.
